title: Rybakina beats Gauff to book US Open final against Sabalenka
text:
Elena Rybakina overpowered Coco Gauff 3-6, 6-4, 6-4 ​in a fierce US Open semifinal to secure a title showdown with defending ​champion Aryna ‌Sabalenka and stay on course for a third major crown.

Gauff absorbed relentless pressure ‌and stayed strong from the ⁠back to draw errors from Rybakina, breaking ​in the ‌sixth game and taking the opening set in front of a roaring crowd that included former first lady ​Michelle ‌Obama.

Rybakina capitalised on some sloppy play by the fourth-seeded American ⁠in the second ‌set to level the ‌match and silence the Arthur Ashe Stadium ‌court.

She gained control with her power and broke ‌to ​go 5-3 ⁠ahead in the deciding set.

Gauff hit back with a break of her own but her comeback bid ⁠faltered when she could not hold serve, as Rybakina ‌broke ‌to close out the ​win.

Sunday's final, AEST, will be a rematch of this year's Australian Open decider, which Rybakina won in three sets.

Aryna Sabalenka dispensed of Jessica Pegula in straight sets. (Getty Imagers: Sarah Stier)

Earlier, Sabalenka eliminated American Jessica Pegula 7-5, 6-2, moving one win away from a rare third consecutive title in New York.

The top seed simmered with frustration early in the match before finding her best level, sending over 29 winners and seven aces before closing it out with an unreturnable shot deep in the American's territory.

Third seed Pegula, runner-up in 2024, had no answer ​to the Belarusian's power and allowed ‌costly mistakes to creep into her game in the second set.

"I was so desperate for the win, I wanted it badly," Sabalenka said.

Tiafoe scores US Open comeback win Ben Shelton has triumphed in a five-set thriller that set a new US Open record as the latest finish ever to a match at the New York grand slam.

Pegula saved an early break point with a fine forehand winner, while Sabalenka ⁠showed signs of frustration, whacking her racquet on the court after a double ‌fault in the ninth game.

Sabalenka threw ​her racquet to the ground ‌as Pegula held her serve in the 10th game, but hit her stride to break her opponent from the baseline on set point.

"I felt like whatever decision I would make, it is the right decision," said Sabalenka, who lost in her last encounter against Pegula at the Berlin semifinals in June.

"I would definitely say that against ⁠Jess probably today, compared to the last matches we played, ‌it was definitely the better level ‌from me."

The defeat ended Pegula's latest campaign for a first major and she questioned whether even her best work ‌could have reversed the result.

"She played insane. She played a super-high level," Pegula said.

"Honestly, I don't really know if there was much I could do today."

Reuters

title: Breaking: Queensland's credit rating downgraded for first time since 2009
text:
Queensland's credit rating has been downgraded for the first time in almost 20 years, putting pressure on the state's multi-billion-dollar debt and Olympic infrastructure.

S&P Global Ratings today confirmed it had lowered its "long-term issuer credit rating" on Queensland to AA from AA+.

The state has had an AA+ rating since early 2009.

In a statement, S&P Global said the outlook on the long-term for the state remains stable.

"The stable outlook on the long-term rating reflects our view that Queensland's budgetary performance will remain weak over the next few years as the state ramps up its infrastructure spending, resulting in debt being structurally higher than in the past," the statement said.

The Queensland government has a big infrastructure bill ahead of the 2032 Olympic Games. (AAP: Jono Searle)

The statement provided an upside and downside scenario for the next few years for Queensland.

"We could lower our long-term rating on Queensland if its financial management weakens," S&P Global said in reference to the downside scenario.

"Weaker management could drive persistent operating deficits and wider deficits after capital accounts, and substantially higher debt."

For the upside, the statement said Queensland's credit rating could be raised if the state "runs sustained operating surpluses and narrower deficits after capital accounts on a continued basis".

Queensland Treasurer David Janetzki has consistently said a downgrade was likely since coming to government in 2024.

Credit agencies expect Queensland to incur large deficits over the next two years. (ABC News: Jessica van Vonderon)

In a statement yesterday, he blamed the potential downgrade on the former Labor government and the impacts from the latest federal budget.

S&P Global Ratings' research update on the state, published in February this year, said it expected the state to incur operating deficits and large deficits after capital accounts over the next two years, before recovering by fiscal 2028.

"As a result, debt will rise steadily but remain lower than most Australian states," the credit agency said.

"The negative outlook reflects our view that Queensland's budgetary performance could weaken during the next two years, resulting in higher debt, largely due to heavy infrastructure spending."

Speaking on 612 ABC Brisbane before the announcement, Federal Treasurer Jim Chalmers disagreed with Mr Janetzki's view that Queensland's budget was under pressure because of the Commonwealth.

Jim Chalmers says it is "absolutely wrong" for David Janetzki to blame the Commonwealth. (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

He said the federal government has been "piling billions and billions of extra dollars" into the state.

"Every budget around Australia, including certainly the Commonwealth budget, is under pressure for one reason or another," Mr Chalmers said on Friday morning.

"But the Queensland budget is not under pressure because of the Commonwealth."

He alluded to the state's downgraded rating in federal parliament yesterday, where he said the risk of a downgrade was "very troubling".

title: Tasmanian sand mine bid to include 700m jetty in the north-east
text:
A company that will next month apply to mine millions of tonnes of sand for export from Tasmania's largest farm says it plans to build a 700-metre jetty that would also support other businesses in the state's remote north-east.

But Aboriginal groups have raised concerns about the environmental and cultural impacts of the project, which would be about 150 metres inland and would depend on the construction of the lengthy jetty for exports.

Tony Ellis, the director of North Scottsdale Resources, said next month the company would lodge its mining lease application to dredge and treat around 90 million to 100 million tonnes of sand, over 30 to 40 years, from a 500-hectare site on Tasmania's north-eastern tip.

He said they were targeting a type of sand used to make concrete, which he said was in short supply across Sydney, Melbourne and Hobart, as well as cities in South-East Asia.

Mr Ellis said the proposed mining area was "wholly enclosed on the Rushy Lagoon property" — Tasmania's largest farm, which recently sold to UK investment firm Gresham House and plans to plant roughly 12 million pine seedlings across it.

North Scottsdale Resources was granted the 15 square kilometre exploration licence in the state's far north east in 2015. (Supplied: The List)

Rushy Lagoon is also slated to host wind turbines as part of ACEN's 210-turbine North East Wind project, which is currently applying for a major project permit.

Gresham House's Tasmanian Natural Asset Trust manager Jonathan Craven said it had had "preliminary discussions with the proponent about the proposed sand mine".

But he said Gresham House was yet to see details of the environmental, cultural and commercial impacts of the project.

Mr Ellis said the proposal would provide dual benefits to the region's other operators, through the construction of a 700-metre jetty, south of Petal Point.

The approximate location of the planned jetty. (Supplied: Tony Ellis)

He said this would be used to load sand onto a transfer vessel, which would transport it over shallow waters to larger ships, "which will carry it to various ports on the mainland, possibly Hobart and also South-East Asia".

North Scottsdale Resource's Tony Ellis say the company plans to mine sand in the state's north-east. (Supplied: Tony Ellis)

But he also said the jetty could have multiple users, suggesting ACEN could use it to bring in bulky wind turbines, or others could use it to transport container freight.

An ACEN Australia spokesperson said the jetty proposed by North Scottsdale Resources was not critical to its development, which would require its own transport solution.

Mr Ellis anticipated the proposed sand mine would initially employ 25-30 people, increasing as production ramped up.

"If we have a day and an evening shift, it could be up around the 40 odd people," he said.

He said the company had undertaken Aboriginal heritage studies and flora and fauna assessments, as well as drilling to assess the quality of the sand and any potential acid sulphate soils that may exist on site.

Tasmanian Aboriginal Centre (TAC) members say they are concerned by a proposal to mine sand near Pupiyala / Boobyalla Beach. (Supplied: Stevie Battese)

Aboriginal groups raise concerns

But the Tasmanian Aboriginal Centre (TAC) and the Melaythenner Teeackana Warrana Aboriginal Corporation (MTWAC) have each separately raised concerns about the environmental impact of the proposed sand mine.

The TAC's country and culture manager Andry Sculthorpe said its members gathered at Pupiyala/Boobyalla Beach yesterday to make their opposition to the project clear.

The Tasmanian Aboriginal Centre members hold a banner saying "country not concrete". (Supplied: Stevie Battese)

"The sandy coastlines of the North East are areas where our ancestors lived their lives and buried their dead," he said.

"They hold layers of history that must not be destroyed. A mine of this scale permanently destroys this country and the heritage it holds.

"Those connections are fundamental to who we are, and we will not allow them to be destroyed."

He said there were serious concerns about the environmental impact of sand mining more broadly, and Tasmania should not volunteer its beaches to feed a "questionable international demand" for sand.

MTWAC co-chair Mark Harriss said his organisation was concerned about the project's size, the ecological impact of the jetty and the vessels it would accommodate, risks to the Boobyalla sand dunes and a plan to progressively transform the mined area into a lake.

Mr Ellis confirmed the lake was part of the company's plan, and said it was investigating whether it could be used for aquaculture or to host solar panels.

He also said waste sand would be used to create wetlands.

But he also said "the coastal dunes will not be touched" and the mining will occur about 150m inland from the dunes on "old degraded agricultural grazing land".

"I think that's an indicator of [the land's] mistreatment rather than its ecological value as a space," Mr Harriss responded.

Calls for broader consultation

Mr Harriss, a pakana man, said while there had been engagement between the parties, Aboriginal community members had not yet been adequately consulted about the project and its potential impacts.

"For us, it's being at the table at every stage around consultation and being involved in what that plan looks like," he said.

Melaythenner Teeackana Warrana Aboriginal Corporation (MTWAC) co-chair Mark Harriss says traditional owners need to be genuinely consulted. (ABC News: Emily Smith)

"We are absolutely in support of industry.

"However, it needs to be done in the right way.

" We need to be consulted genuinely. "

He said the company's Aboriginal heritage assessment needed to be coupled with "meaningful, deliberate and comprehensive engagement" with Aboriginal people, which would allow them to provide free, prior and informed consent.

Melaythenner Teeackana Warrana Aboriginal Corporation (MTWAC) co-chair Mark Harriss likes to keep a fire burning near their base. (ABC News: Emily Smith)

He called on the Dorset Council, which will eventually assess the proposal, to ensure proper consultation occurred.

A state government spokesperson said Mineral Resources Tasmania was "engaging directly with members of the local Aboriginal community to address their concerns over future activity near sensitive areas".

Mr Ellis said he was "more than happy" to sit down with concerned parties for further consultation.

He said North Scottsdale Resources had held an exploration permit over the area since 2015, and planned to lodge its mining lease application next month.

He guessed the earliest it could be approved for mining was late 2027.

title: No traffic lights from Melbourne to Coffs as M1 'missing link' opens
text:
Drivers can now travel from Melbourne to the NSW mid north coast without passing a single traffic light, after the opening of a $2.24 billion M1 extension.

The new 15-kilometre stretch of motorway at Raymond Terrace includes two lanes in each direction, 11 new bridges over surrounding flood plains and bypasses both Hexham and Heatherbrae altogether.

Both locations have been bottlenecks for decades, with large volumes of freight and holiday traffic merging with local commuters, bringing movement to a standstill during peak periods.

The new motorway is expected to shave off up to 9 minutes of travel time and take up to 25,000 vehicles off local roads every day.

Plans for the extension were first lodged in 2004, and the project has often been referred to as the "missing link" in Australia's east coast road network.

Dennis Roohan manages a trucking company in Beresfield, near the end of the M1.

Dennis Roohan says the new road will save truck drivers significant time. (ABC Newcastle: Tamara Penniket)

Speaking to ABC Newcastle Drive he described the extension as "a game changer" estimating it would save truck drivers significant time on their long-haul trips up north.

"[The bottlenecks] add a considerable length of time to the driver's journey each day," he said.

"The drivers will now be home earlier to their families and then it's got the whole knock-on effect for the whole area of Beresfield.

" To get our local roads back will be good. "

The new road has also been touted as an economic boost for the Hunter and NSW North Coast.

"This so much more than a road project," said Committee for the Hunter CEO Alice Thompson.

"It's about strengthening connections between the Hunter and North Coast and the Sydney to Brisbane corridor

"This supports people, freight, tourism, investment and jobs … a great day,."

The M1 extension is expected to shave off up to 9 minutes of travel time and take up to 25,000 vehicles off local roads every day. (Supplied: Transport for NSW)

The Coalition government committed $1.6 billion to the project under Scott Morrison in 2019, and successive state and federal governments have continued to add to the funding bucket, with construction officially starting in 2023.

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese visited the Hunter region earlier this week to cut the ribbon on the final $2.24 billion project.

"Everyone who's ever driven from Sydney to Brisbane will all know that this choke point was something that was a real issue," he said.

"It's great for locals because what it will do is make sure that it separates out the highway from local roads, which is good for road safety."

Anthony Albanese cut the ribbon on the new motorway earlier this week. (ABC Newcastle: Ben Clifford)

Ahead of schedule

The project was due to open to traffic in 2028, but a large workforce of more than 2,700 workers, streamlined decisions and good weather are being credited with bringing the completion date forward by 18 months.

"There is a little bit of luck of the weather in it," NSW Roads Minister Jenny Aitchison said.

"But I think it's just really a testament to the team.

"We've had 70 per cent of the workforce here as locals, so they can see the urgency and the need for this project," she said.

With the project complete, motorists travelling from Melbourne will not hit a single traffic light until they reach Coffs Harbour. (ABC Newcastle: Tamara Penniket)

With the new motorway now open to traffic, motorists travelling from Melbourne to Queensland won't pass a single set of traffic lights until they hit Coffs Harbour.

Those lights will be removed from the trip when the Coffs Harbour bypass opens at the end of the year.

The M1 to Raymond Terrace extension is now open to traffic in both directions. (ABC Newcastle: Tamara Penniket)

The Coalition has welcomed the opening, but neighbouring Nationals MP for the seat of Lyne, Alison Penfold, said other parts of the road network still needed serious attention.

"It's great to celebrate the M1 extension, but I just don't want governments now to say 'job done'," she said.

"There's at least six grade-separated interchanges and overpasses that are still needed [on the Pacific Highway].

"Now we've finished one job let's get on to the next," she said.

title: Sydney Roosters claim NRLW minor premiership after another perfect season
text:
The Bulldogs have flirted with the biggest upset in NRLW history before the undefeated Roosters charged home in the final 20 minutes for a 42-12 win at the Sydney Football Stadium.

Entering last night's game in Sydney with just three wins all year and having conceded 178 points in four consecutive losses, the Bulldogs led until the 52nd minute, only to run out of steam with strike centre Monica Tagoai in the sin bin.

While they were far from their best, it was a 26th consecutive regular-season win for master coach John Strange's Roosters side, who remain on track to reclaim the premiership they lost to the Broncos last year, with their only loss in round five of 2024.

The Roosters will now enjoy the bye afforded to the top two teams in week one of the six-team finals format.

Despite being huge underdogs, the visitors had the early ascendancy, and it took almost 12 minutes before Otesa Pule crossed for the Roosters to get the scoreboard ticking.

It did not take long after that for Corban Baxter to slip a gem of a pass to Jessica Sergis, who ran 40 metres to score her competition-leading 15th try of the season.

Just when it looked like the floodgates would open, the Bulldogs worked their way back down the field, and Tagoai powered her way over to bring her side within four points with 10 minutes left in the half.

Seven minutes later, the Dogs' five-eighth Andie Robinson flew high over Baxter to pluck a pinpoint Tayla Preston bomb from the air and touch down.

With Preston's conversion, they were surprise 12-10 leaders at the break, leaving the shortest-priced favourites in NRLW history shell-shocked.

To make matters worse for the Roosters, Baxter left the field at half-time for a head injury assessment and failed to return after the interval.

The Bulldogs stayed on top for the opening 13 minutes of the second stanza, before Tagoai was sin-binned by referee Karra-Lee Nolan for a hip-drop.

Five minutes later, Isabelle Kelly, starting in her 50th game as captain of the Roosters, tore through the middle of the Dogs' defence and found prop Millie Elliott in support for the competition leaders to reclaim the lead.

Taina Naividi was next over the stripe and Canterbury's dream was over.

More tries followed to Pule, Mia Woods, Sergis and Jocelyn Kelleher for a final score that somewhat flattered the minor premiers.

Despite the loss, it was a brave effort from the Bulldogs and coach Brayden Wiliame, in his final game at the helm before Mark O'Meley takes the reins in 2027.

title: Mining safety regulator warns against 'unprecedented' vapes in mines
text:
An unprecedented number of reports of contraband, such as vapes, being brought into coalmines are being investigated by Resources Safety and Health Queensland (RSHQ).

The regulator has issued a safety alert reminding workers to be vigilant when checking their personal belongings before entering mines, and to surrender any prohibited items.

A vape pulled apart showing the heating elements and battery inside. (Supplied: Resources Safety and Health Queensland)

Kerri Melkersson, executive director of the Safety in Mines Testing and Research Station, said contraband created an "unacceptable ignition risk".

"Underground coal mines may contain methane gas and combustible coal dust," she said.

"So, any ignition source has the potential to trigger a fire or a catastrophic explosion, which obviously can cause multiple injuries, even fatalities."

Kerri Melkersson, Executive Director of Safety in Mines Testing and Research Station. (Supplied: Resources Safety and Health Queensland)

After testing vapes, Ms Melkersson found the devices to be exceptionally powerful.

"Some people may say, 'Look, it's just a vape, how dangerous can it be?'" she said.

"What we were able to demonstrate was that the heating elements inside vapes can reach temperatures in excess of 250 degrees Celsius when they're in use.

" They can generate over 100 times more energy than is necessary to ignite gas in an underground coal mine. "

Researchers at RSHQ tested the vapes. (Supplied: Resources Safety and Health Queensland)

The RSHQ has received six reports of contraband materials in mines in the past five months, including watches, mobile phones, and smoking materials.

Until this year, RSHQ had never received any reports of miners bringing vapes into mines.

The body hadn't received reports of any contraband entering underground coal mines since 2012.

An incident involving an e-cigarette exploding in a West Australian mine left a worker with severe burns and was compared to "fireworks going off".

Batteries inside vapes can trigger explosions in mines. (Supplied: Resources Safety and Health Queensland)

Ms Melkersson urged operators to continue checking their procedures.

"Supervisors need to be checking their workers' understanding and, basically, operators need to continue to check the effectiveness of their controls," she said.

"The message has to be really clear: no vapes, no lighters, no contraband underground."

title: Resort says sale or refinancing will address 'outstanding' superannuation
text:
Former Rumi on Louth staff and customers have expressed concern about outstanding super and voucher entitlements, as the island is listed for sale.

The millionaire co-owner of the award-winning South Australian island resort has acknowledged some former workers' "superannuation contributions remain outstanding" and will be addressed "through either the refinancing or sale process", but has insisted that does not change plans for re-opening and expansion.

The $30-million eco-resort, located 10 minutes from Port Lincoln by boat, is run by Ika Shima Pty Ltd trading as Rumi on Louth and faces a clouded future after being listed for sale earlier this month.

The Rumi on Louth resort includes a restaurant, accommodation and outdoor experiences accessible through a buggy. (Supplied: Rumi on Louth)

Co-owner and director of Ika Shima Pty Ltd Che Metcalfe opened the sprawling retreat, which includes accommodation, fine dining and outdoor experiences, in 2023 but temporarily shut the doors in May while investigating how to fund the development's second stage.

Outstanding super 'taken seriously', owner says

Port Lincoln visa worker Scott Houston told ABC Eyre Peninsula Breakfast that he is owed "a couple of grand" in superannuation and is now looking for another sponsor to remain in Australia.

He said the sudden dismissal was "devastating" and questioned if the resort would reopen.

"If it didn't work the first time, how could it work the second time?" he said.

"You've cut off some of the best employees you could have had, how could you possibly reopen?"

Scott Houston (right) during his time working at Rumi on Louth. (Supplied: Scott Houston)

In a statement, Mr Metcalfe said Rumi on Louth "temporarily paused operations … while pursuing recapitalisation and planning for stage 2 expansion" and was "concurrently exploring the sale of Louth Island".

Rumi on Louth resort co-owner Che Metcalfe. (Supplied: LinkedIn)

"All employees were paid their wages, accrued leave and other termination entitlements when operations paused," he said.

"Some superannuation contributions remain outstanding, which we take seriously, and intend to address through either the refinancing or sale process."

Voucher holders ask for refunds

A two-night stay for two guests starts at $2,062, while a three-night stay for two during the peak New Year period costs $5,080.

With the price tag, the closure has unsettled some gift voucher holders, including Susan Thompson and mother Margaret Harvey.

"It's a substantial amount of money toward what was meant to be a special occasion," Ms Thompson said.

"Now, we're in a position, as I know many within our community are, that we don't know, firstly, if we'll be able to use our vouchers, and secondly, when."

Margaret Harvey and Susan Thompson had planned to visit the resort for a family gathering. (Supplied: Margaret Harvey)

Ms Harvey said at first, the resort told her there would be "the possibility of a refund". Then it said she had been provided incorrect information and extended the voucher's expiry date.

She described the company's communication as "disappointing", having taken two weeks to respond to questions about the voucher's validity.

In response, Mr Metcalfe said "all existing Rumi vouchers have been extended by 12 months, and our intention remains to honour them when operations resume".

"If the business is ultimately unable to honour those vouchers, they will be refunded," Mr Metcalfe said.

"Given the confidential nature of current processes and privacy of individual employment matters, I don't intend to comment further on speculation or individual circumstances."

He also said the company's vessels, used to ferry visitors over, "have not been sold and remain with the business".

title: App owner who lost discrimination case after barring trans woman denied appeal
text:
The founder of a women-only app has been refused special leave to challenge a ruling that found excluding a transgender woman from the platform was discriminatory.

The High Court decision, published on Thursday, shuts down the final avenue of appeal in the landmark case of the Giggle for Girls app and Roxanne Tickle, who was previously awarded $20,000 in damages by the Federal Court.

It was the first case to claim discrimination on the basis of gender identity since changes to the Sex Discrimination Act in 2013.

Sall Grover, Giggle's founder and chief executive officer, sought to have the case heard by the High Court following an appeal outcome in May, which doubled the original damages of $10,000 and found there was direct rather than indirect discrimination.

The chief executive of the female-only app Giggle for Girls, Sall Grover, barred Roxanne Tickle in 2021. (ABC News: ABC News: Liam Patrick)

The High Court said there was no reason to doubt the Full Court's construction of the relevant section of the legislation.

"Any appeal dependent on the demonstration of error in the Full Court's construction of those provisions has insufficient prospects of success to warrant a grant of special leave to appeal," the judges said.

Special leave was refused with costs.

App used AI to distinguish facial features

The Federal Court previously heard Ms Tickle accessed Giggle in 2021 after a registration process that required the uploading of a selfie.

The app, which was marketed as a digital women-only safe space, used artificial intelligence software designed to distinguish between the facial appearance of men and women.

Ms Tickle had access to the app between February and September that year, but her account was then restricted following a manual review.

The Giggle for Girls app was marketed as a platform exclusively for women to share experiences. (AAP)

Ms Grover contended that sex referred to a person's sex at birth.

Ms Tickle has lived as a woman since mid-2017, had her birth certificate reissued with a female sex marker and has undergone gender-affirming surgery, the Federal Court heard.

Ms Grover's lawyers unsuccessfully attempted to invoke a carve-out of discrimination law which exempts measures designed to achieve substantive equality between men and women.

title: Apartment buyer facing $40k shortfall as Bathla collapse puts discount offer at risk
text:
When May agreed to buy an off-the-plan apartment for around $800,000 in north-west Sydney a few years ago, an offer from the developer to reduce the price by 5 per cent as part of the deal was central to her decision.

Today, her apartment remains under construction, the property developer behind it has collapsed, and there is no guarantee Bathla's discount will apply.

May, a first-generation Filipino-Australian whose name has been changed because she fears speaking publicly could affect her dealings with the selling agent and her property purchase, said she and her husband had been wanting to buy their first home for many years but struggled to save a large enough deposit.

ABC Business Daily: Breaking down Bathla Bathla Group has collapsed owing billions, with hundreds of projects caught up in the fallout. Was it simply a company that grew too fast and took on too much debt — or is it a sign of deeper pressure across property and construction?

May said she first came across Bathla's Marsden Park development through a Filipino community Facebook page, where she saw a post promoting low-deposit home ownership, with buyers able to exchange contracts with as little as $5,600 and pay the remainder through an interest-free payment plan with the developer.

She said she learned about the 5 per cent Bathla developer discount payable at settlement after enquiring and meeting with agents from Paragon Realty Group.

ABC News has seen screenshots of communications between May and the sales agent, which repeatedly refer to an arrangement under which May would pay a 5 per cent deposit and the developer would contribute a further 5 per cent at settlement — worth around $40,000.

In one message, the agent described the developer's contribution as a "5 per cent discount", while another referred to the "developer contributing another 5 per cent at settlement".

A WhatsApp message to May referred to Bathla's offer as a "discount". (Supplied)

'I trusted them'

After Bathla entered voluntary administration last month, May asked whether the developer's 5 per cent contribution would still be honoured. The agent said they were seeking clarification from the administrators about how the "5 per cent incentive" would be dealt with.

Paragon was also their main point of contact for other parts of the purchase, May said, telling them legal services could be arranged through the agency and that it had an in-house mortgage broker as well.

May said she only reviewed the contract carefully when Bathla entered administration on August 25, and that was when she discovered the developer contribution was not included in the document.

"Looking back, of course, I wish I had checked the document, but I was promised by the agent, and I trusted them," she said.

" If not for this deal, we would never have purchased this apartment. "

An artist's impression of the Bathla development in Marsden Park. (Supplied)

She now does not know whether Bathla will honour the contribution. If it is not, she and her husband could have to find around $40,000.

"We're just not prepared for it. We don't know how we can manage," May said.

The South St Marsden Park development has been taken over by private credit lender, Leda, owned by billionaire Bob Ell.

The project does not fall in the current short-term funding arrangement backed by five Bathla lenders.

Do you know more? If you have more information about this article or any other tips, you can securely contact reporter Lin Lin at lin.lin@abc.net.au or linreporting@proton.me.

May said she was told that the apartment was expected to be completed in early 2025, but the date had been pushed back several times and is now expected to settle in February 2027. Bathla Group's insolvency complicates the picture.

"That's pretty much what we talk and think about daily. Daily, like every minute," she said.

May is seeking confirmation the contribution will be honoured.

Residential developer Bathla entered voluntary administration in August with debts of more than $3 billion. (AAP: Dan Himbrechts)

Contract leaves buyer in difficult position

University of Sydney law professor Jason Harris said the contract in question required the buyer to pay the full deposit and contained an "entire agreement" clause, under which the buyer acknowledged they had not relied on promises outside the written agreement.

"This makes it very difficult for the buyer to enforce the 5 per cent promise under contract law," Professor Harris said.

However, he said that did not necessarily leave the purchaser without legal arguments.

Depending on the circumstances, possible avenues could include the legal concepts of estoppel or set-off.

Estoppel, for example, can prevent a person from enforcing their strict legal rights where doing so would be unconscionable because of an earlier promise or representation, but the wording of messages and other correspondence would be important in establishing exactly what was promised and who made the representation.

An artist's impression of the Marsden Park development by Bathla. (Supplied)

Independent advice urged

Solicitor Jessie Icao said buyers should obtain legal advice independent of the developer, agent, broker, or other parties involved in a sale.

Developer suspends 60pc of workforce The floundering property developer Bathla Group stands down 213 staff as it secures two weeks' worth of additional funding to continue construction at some of its construction sites.

"You really need, before signing the contract, to see a solicitor, an independent solicitor or an independent conveyancer who can really explain the terms and conditions of the contract," he said.

"I do work with many first-generation migrants, and it is an issue that arises as they are unfamiliar with complexities of buying property in Australia, and will sometimes rely on the selling point given to them by sales agents."

Looking back, May said obtaining independent legal advice was "something that we should have done at that time".

The ABC has not established how many purchasers received the same 5 per cent offer as May.

The ABC has contacted Paragon Realty Group, Bathla Group and Bathla's voluntary administrators, Teneo, about the incentive and whether outstanding offers would be honoured. No responses were received before publication.

Previously, the administrators, Teneo, said they were in the early stages of a full reconciliation of deposits, but that the matter was complex and would take time.

title: Luke Sayers apologises as ex-wife's lewd photo defamation case settles
text:
A protracted legal fight between former Carlton president Luke Sayers and his ex-wife over a lewd photo has reached settlement, with Mr Sayers apologising and acknowledging his former partner never posted the photo.

The image of Mr Sayers's penis was posted on his X (formerly Twitter) account in January 2025, leading him to step down as Carlton president.

Mr Sayers denied posting the photo, saying his account was hacked.

His then-wife Cate sued him for defamation a year later, alleging he provided a statutory declaration to AFL investigators falsely stating that she was responsible for accessing the account and publishing the picture.

In the Supreme Court on Friday, Mr Sayers's legal counsel Sandip Mukerjea read a statement from Mr Sayers saying he apologised "unreservedly" to his wife and acknowledged the "hurt and harm" she had faced.

He said he accepted she did not post the photo.

Mr Sayers was not at the brief hearing.

In a statement outside court, Ms Sayers said she was pleased with the outcome and had started the legal proceedings to establish the truth.

"I acknowledge Luke's public apology to me today, including his clear statement that I was not responsible for posting an explicit image on his X account," she said.

"This brings to a close a painful and difficult chapter that began with extraordinary claims made about me that were accepted without challenge by powerful institutions and powerful people."

Luke and Cate Sayers pictured at the Brownlow Medal ceremony in September 2023. (AAP: James Ross)

She said she'd been overwhelmed by the support of many women whose reputations had been treated as "expendable" and thanked them.

She wouldn't disclose if there was a financial settlement as part of the deal.

High-profile saga comes to an end

The agreement brings an end to a very public saga that had played out across the media, especially in football-mad Melbourne, over the past year.

Earlier this year, Mr Sayers had applied to have the case transferred to the Federal Circuit and Family Court, a move that would have effectively prevented media reporting of the case.

He failed in that bid, but Friday’s settlement means that any more details about what happened between the couple will not be aired.

The photo posted on Mr Sayers's X account on January 8 last year — while he was in Italy with his then-wife and daughters — was quickly deleted, but not before it was screenshotted by other social media users.

In court documents, Mr Sayers claimed the post was made while he was in the shower.

An inquiry launched by the AFL cleared Mr Sayers of breaching AFL rules and found, on the available evidence, that access to his account "was compromised".

Ms Sayers had argued her ex-husband made numerous false claims in his statutory declaration to the AFL, including information about her mental health and sexual history, and that she was residing in the same apartment as Mr Sayers at the time of the controversial X post.

She also argued the AFL investigation was inadequate because she was never interviewed, nor was Mr Sayers's phone forensically examined.

In response, Mr Sayers denied leaking details of his statutory declaration to the media and accused his wife of accessing his phone in March 2025 and viewing and copying confidential material.

Mr Sayers is a former chief executive of PwC and was in charge when the firm was embroiled in a tax scandal after a staff member misused confidential government information.

title: Having a toilet at work shouldn't be news, but in the construction industry it is
text:
Toilets and sanitary disposal bins should be a given at work, but many women in the construction industry are having to leave a job to go to the loo.

Temperley Homes director Carly Dewey has been in the construction industry for more than 15 years and said basic facilities for women "should be the norm".

"It would be nice if it was not even a conversation," Ms Dewey said.

"We make up half the population. We should be in construction."

The builder said she organises male and female toilets with serviced sanitary disposal bins on all her building sites.

"It is male-dominated, so people probably only think about the boys, and also the cost, because essentially we have to pay for two toilets plus the sanitary bins, but to us it's just another job cost," Ms Dewey said.

Many Canberra women in construction are having to leave work to find a toilet. (ABC News: David Scaisci)

She said the extra facilities were about $150 a week to hire, with a little extra for servicing and transporting the sanitary bins.

But she said it was a small price compared to the cost of losing a worker's time.

"The cost of having labour leave to have to go to the bathroom and come back versus the cost of having a toilet here. I think it's a no-brainer to have a toilet to serve the girls," she said.

She said she understood it was easier for commercial construction employers to provide more facilities "but residential is hard because often the margins are smaller and there are smaller crews".

'Lucky if you get a portaloo'

Electrician Lainey Morgan says she has seen improvements at some sites, but it is inconsistent. (ABC News: David Sciasci )

Not every site gets it right, according to electrician Lainey Morgan, who has worked across residential and commercial jobs in Canberra.

"I'm finding that there is a lot more sanitation, like sanitary products provided, which is great, especially on some sites," she said.

"But [for] others you're lucky if you get a portaloo."

She said inadequate facilities had a direct impact on her work.

"I think it affects productivity. I find if there aren't adequate facilities on site, then I'm usually having to go and find public facilities off site," Ms Morgan said.

" You're having to drive somewhere else and then come back … it's a big disruption to workflow. "

Ms Morgan said the problem was not confined to residential builds, and came down to individual businesses rather than the sector as a whole.

Speaking up as an apprentice

Sanitary disposal bins in toilets on construction sites are often not provided by employers. (ABC News: David Sciasci)

Ms Morgan said the bigger issue was often cultural, particularly for early-career women in construction.

She recalled being the only woman on some of her first sites as an apprentice.

"Unless I had personally said something, which can be really intimidating to speak up about, then there would just be no facilities," she said.

"I think there's still a very big culture in apprentices not being able to speak up about stuff like this.

"They're almost like criticised for discussing something like basic needs."

Ms Morgan and Ms Dewey said they wanted to see facilities become an automatic part of setting up a site, rather than something women had to request.

"Less needing women to start the conversation about something that is healthcare and is a necessity and something that's basic hygiene," Ms Morgan said.

What does the law say?

Worksafe ACT has a code that legally requires employers to provide toilets and washing facilities that are clean, safe, maintained and accessible to all workers.

ACT Work Health and Safety Commissioner Jacqueline Agius said inspectors had substantiated some confronting accounts from workers.

"We have heard stories of people who have nowhere to dispose of their sanitary products, and wrap them up in toilet paper, put them in their pockets and carry them around for the whole day until they get home," she said.

"We've heard stories of people not being able to change their sanitary products, not having a suitable and private place to do that."

Tradies quitting over onsite toilets Tradies are walking out. Not over ability or aptitude but toilets — in a symbol of the sector's persistent barriers.

She said poorly maintained portable toilets were a particular problem on residential construction sites.

"Particularly in residential construction in new builds, the portaloos — they're not maintained, and so they can get really grotty and pretty filthy, and no one's going to use those," Ms Agius said.

But she said the problem was not limited to construction and the regulator had received complaints across a range of industries over the past 12 months.

She said inadequate facilities could also mean something as basic as being unable to wash your hands.

Ms Agius said where inspectors found a workplace falling short, the businesses were given a legal directive to fix it.

Cultural shift underway

Master Builders ACT chief executive Anna Neelagama says she wants to see more women in construction. (ABC News: Callum Flinn)

Master Builders ACT chief executive Anna Neelagama said improving facilities for women would help grow the female workforce in construction.

"A big focus for us is improving the number of women participating in the construction workforce," Ms Neelagama said.

"So obviously having appropriate sanitation facilities is a key part of that."

Ms Neelagama pointed to the organisation's Level the Site program, which she said supported employers to promote gender-inclusive workplace culture.

"[It] works with employers to look at the whole workplace experience, including making sure you do have those sanitation facilities, because it's safer and more productive," she said.

title: Neil Armfield on Death of a Salesman's relevance to a modern world for sale
text:
It's fair to say a lot has changed since American playwright Arthur Miller wrote Death of a Salesman in 1948.

The American dream still sells the promise of the world, yet with global populations having exploded by 240 per cent since, it's put at risk much of what made it beautiful in the first place.

From nature covered by packaging and pollution, to unsustainable living trends and popular music commodified into formulaic trash, capitalism's finely tuned mechanisms seem impossible to stop.

Ben O'Toole, Anthony Lapaglia and Josh Helman perform in the 2026 Australian season of Death of a Salesman. (Supplied: Jeff Busby)

The promises keep coming — a bigger car, a flashier phone, trendier clothes, higher social status — sold to us by brash world leaders as people struggle to pay the bills and wealth distribution grows increasingly inequitable.

Amid this backdrop, Miller's play about a tired, broke and increasingly deluded salesman seems as relevant as ever.

"He's written this extraordinary play about the collapse of America, or predicting the collapse of America, which we're seeing acted out in real time today," Death of a Salesman Australia director Neil Armfield OA said.

"It's a society that has deep roots in something great, but is able to be lost by these kind of confidence tricksters."

Arthur Miller won the Pulitzer Prize for Drama for Death of a Salesman. (AFP)

Even some of the lines by lead character, salesman Willy Logan, sound familiar.

"In a sense, the play comes in sideways at this enormous malaise and this whole notion of a society built on sales, where, as Willy says, 'It's not what you say; it's how you say it,' or, 'Start big and you'll end big,'" Armfield said.

"There are all these kind of Trumpian tropes that are seen as sources of glory for this guy, who is dying as we watch him proceed through the play."

But Miller's play is not about politics. It is centred on family and domestic issues.

Told largely through arguments, memories and a final ditch to improve their lot, it presents the salesman's collapsing career, his shortcomings as a father and husband, and his failure to achieve the great American dream despite a lifetime in its pursuit.

Alison Whyte plays Linda Loman in the Australian season of Death of a Salesman. (Supplied: Jeff Busby)

"The other centre of gravity in the play is Biff, Willy's eldest son who grew up loving him, and was all set to be the incarnation of his father's sense of the glory of America, but who sees, at a crucial moment, through the lies," Armfield said.

"He's only 34 but has been trying to reconcile his own love of nature, of the truth and his own sense of self, with the kind of dreams that got pumped into him by his father and which he feels he can never live up to.

" So there's this heartbreaking guy who is finding what it really means to be human, to be a moral person and a loving son, to a father who is lost inside the lie of the American dream. "

Miller's play premiered on Broadway in 1949 and ran for 742 performances, receiving the Pulitzer Prize for Drama and a Tony Award for Best Play.

It has been revived on Broadway six times.

An Australian hit

Armfield's Australian production of Death of a Salesman premiered at Her Majesty's Theatre in Melbourne during 2023.

It was revived at Theatre Royal Sydney in 2024 and, after returning to Melbourne this year before a season in Brisbane, finishes with its Adelaide season starting later this month.

Alison Whyte on Death of a Salesman After rave reviews for past seasons, Alison Whyte returns to play Linda Loman opposite Anthony LaPaglia in Arthur Miller's classic play.

Led by Adelaide-born actor Anthony LaPaglia as Willy, Alison Whyte as Linda Loman, Josh Helman as Biff, and Ben O'Toole — who came on board when it was revived for the Sydney season in 2024 — as Happy, it has retained the same leading cast.

Armfield said the production had become "richer" with each season.

"I think what [producer] Torben Brookman realised was that there was a real hunger in audiences for classic plays that were being kind of ignored by the state companies," he said.

"That's not a criticism. Different companies are contributing to the culture in different ways.

"But it meant that there was an audience hungry to see a great play and a beautiful production."

Neil Armfield and Rachel Healy during their tenures as Adelaide Festival co-directors. (891 ABC Adelaide: Malcolm Sutton)

Armfield is from Sydney's western suburbs, but has a long history working in Adelaide.

Most recently this year he directed Cinderella at Her Majesty's Theatre, and in 2022 directed the oratorio, Watershed: The Death of Doctor Duncan, in the Dunstan Playhouse.

Gay hate crime retold onstage The 1972 murder of a man in Adelaide sparked gay law reform. He is now being memorialised on stage.

Armfield, who says he has directed plays in all of South Australia's major theatres after coming to the city in the 80s with "the magnificent State Theatre Company", also directed A German Life in 2021 at the Playhouse.

"Adelaide was where I learnt to work on a big stage," he said.

He also co-directed seven Adelaide Festivals with Rachel Healy from 2017, wanting to give back to the city's performing arts scene and "the incredible potential that was released here in the 70s and 80s".

Death of a Salesman runs from September 26 to October 4 at the Adelaide Festival Centre.

title: The innovative and lucrative athletics format sidelining some of its stars
text:
World Athletics is set for its latest attempt at a slimmed-down, cashed-up event, with the so-called Ultimate Championship starting Saturday morning (AEST) in Budapest.

The event starts less than a week after the conclusion of the Diamond League season, with all the bells and whistles expected from a track and field meet trying to cut through on a global stage.

Winners will receive US$150,000 ($209,530) and even the eighth-placed athletes picking up a six-figure pay cheque as part of an overall US$10 million ($14 million) purse.

Held over three straight night sessions, the track at Hungary's Gyula Zsivotzky National Athletics Centre will illuminate to highlight the event happening in that moment.

Rather than a lengthy program including qualifying runs, there will be just one final for many events and semis in the 100m, 200m, 400m and hurdles races.

Loading Instagram content

In a year without an Olympics or world championships, World Athletics president Sebastian Coe said the event will answer a simple but important question.

"Who's the best?" he said.

"Nobody goes into the sport to figure out who's second best, they go in wanting to know who the best is. And I think at the end of these championships we will have gone a long way to identifying that."

To confirm that, there will be no podiums, only weighty prize purses and bragging rights between the 381 fierce competitors.

Patterson claims Diamond League final title Eleanor Patterson continues her outstanding season by winning the women's high jump at the Diamond League Final in Brussels.

Most of the traditional track events will be contested (although 3,000m steeplechase, 10,000m and race walking are out) with only Olympic gold medallists, world champions and the current top-ranked athletes invited.

That includes Australian sprint stars Lachlan Kennedy in the 100m and Torrie Lewis in the 200m; Sarah Billings in the 800m; Abbey Caldwell, Jessica Hull and Cameron Myers in the 1,500m; and Ky Robinson, Rose Davies and Hull in the 5,000m.

Diamond League winner Eleanor Patterson and world champion Nicola Olyslagers will compete in the women's high jump, while Commonwealth Games gold medallists Kurtis Marchall (pole vault) and Mackenzie Little (javelin) are also competing.

As part of the hype around the meet, World Athletics held a catwalk fashion event before a televised lane draft for the 200m, allowing athletes to choose which heat and lane they will run in.

Torrie Lewis will race in a stacked semifinal heat. (Getty Images: Mattia Ozbot/World Athletics)

The draft order was based on world rankings, with American Olympic champion Gabby Thomas picking first and placing herself in lane seven of the first semifinal heat.

World 100m and 200m champion Melissa Jefferson-Wooden, made the next selection and placed herself right inside her US teammate, kicking off the mind games early.

Lewis, choosing 10th, selected the outside lane in that first race and immediately going up against the best of the best.

"It is the confidence for me," 2008 Olympic 100m hurdles gold medallist Dawn Harper-Nelson said as she hosted the event.

"This is what the lane draft is about."

Coe said the innovations on display would show what the sport can be in the future, but that may sound some alarm bells for those athletes and disciplines without an invitation to Budapest.

Discus did not make the cut for the Ultimate Championship. (Getty Images: Dean Mouhtaropoulos)

The field program is very restrictive, with men's and women's events for high jump, javelin, long jump and pole vault, while only men's hammer throw and women's triple jump made the cut.

That left many on the outside looking in, including Australian discus star Matt Denny, who said the Ultimate Championship highlighted "a bigger issue in our sport".

The payday and spotlight could be life changing for track and field athletes who travel the world to compete without many opportunities for the sort of prize money afforded to other sports stars.

"I support the concept of the Ultimate Championships," Denny wrote on Instagram.

"Athletics needs innovation. We need to improve the broadcast product, attract new audiences and find better ways to grow the sport.

"But innovation should not come at the expense of opportunity."

Loading Instagram content

The main argument for the disciplines that were included boiled down to a lack of audience interest in those that missed out, but Denny said that was an unfair metric when it is not athletes who make broadcasting decisions.

"When events are minimally shown on broadcasts for the last 20 years, you lose the reasoning to say people don't want to watch," he wrote.

"You cannot control what gets shown, what gets promoted, whose stories are told and which events receive the greatest exposure, then simply point to the result numbers as proof that people do not care about everything else.

"If an event is struggling for attention, before deciding the event is the problem, we should be asking whether we have genuinely given it the opportunity to succeed."

The post received praise from fellow omitted athletes like Australian hammer throw national champion Steph Ratcliffe, race walker Rhydian Cowley and American shot put great Chase Jackson.

But even invited athletes like Dutch 400m star Lieke Klaver and European javelin champion Julian Weber backed Denny's sentiments, with Weber praising the post as "so true".

Over the past four decades, Nicole Lynch has watched motor neurone disease strip her family members of their agency and rob years from their lives. In 1995, her cousin was diagnosed with MND. Not long after, so was another cousin. Her mother died from MND at the age of 51, and her family suspects it killed both of her grandparents on her mother’s side too. Lynch will be one of the beneficiaries of the PBS listing of a new treatment for a rare form of ALS. James Brickwood “It’s awful … The worst thing about it is knowing what’s going to happen,” the 54-year-old said. Her family carries a gene mutation that causes amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS). While ALS is the most common form of MND – the same disease that killed AFL great Neale Daniher – only 2 per cent of people with MND will suffer from this particular mutation.

Advertisement

Related Article Health Bronte calls for her mum in the dark of night, scared of dying. There is no cure for her condition Lynch’s 25-year-old daughter carries the gene mutation. For the first time, patients with the rare form of MND will be able to access a new treatment on the PBS that could extend their lifespan by years. From October 1, Tofersen will be subsidised on the national scheme. Professor Dominic Rowe is a clinical neurologist who treats several patients with Tofersen. He said the treatment was able to change the progression of disease in people with SOD1-related MND. When SOD1 mutates, Rowe explains, it acquires what is known as a “toxic gain of function”.

Advertisement

This means the gene – which, in a body without MND, usually protects cells from damage – instead begins attacking and gradually destroying motor neurons in the brain and spine. “What the therapy does is reduce the amount of toxic protein in a patient’s motor neurons, and by reducing that toxic protein, improves the ability of motor neurons to survive, and slows the progression of their loss,” Rowe said. “When you slow the progression of motor neuron loss, you slow the progression of weakness, ultimately translating into improved quality of life and improved survival.” Lynch, who was diagnosed with MND in December 2021, travels from the mid-North Coast to Sydney every three weeks to receive the treatment she describes as “life-changing”. Her team administers local anaesthetic before injecting a dose of Tofersen via a lumbar puncture that sends the fluid directly into the central nervous system. Lynch spends the night in hospital recovering.

Advertisement

She started the treatment in March 2022, and said her deterioration had come to “a standstill”. A patient diagnosed with MND is expected, on average, to live just two years beyond their diagnosis. Lynch has survived almost five. “I see the treatment as my best friend,” she said. She walks with a limp due to muscular atrophy caused by the disease, so her left calf is much skinnier than her right. Between 35 and 40 per cent of MND patients experience their first symptoms in the lower limbs. Lynch fears, more than anything, how her loss of independence will burden her children in the future.

Advertisement

“Walking up and down stairs is extremely difficult,” she said. “Having to ask people for help, it sucks. It’s like, hang on, I’m the wife and the mother, I should be doing that … It’s the simple things. “I have really dark days. But I keep it to myself. I don’t like upsetting other people, I don’t want to be a burden.” Patients will now pay a maximum of $25 per script for Tofersen. Concession cardholders will pay just $7.70. Before the subsidy, it cost patients up to $28,600 per dose. It is the second treatment for MND listed on the PBS by the Albanese government, and the third overall.

Advertisement

“MND is a heartbreaking, insidious disease that Australians are all too familiar with,” Health Minister Mark Butler said on Friday. Health Minister Mark Butler. Dominic Lorrimer MND Australia chief executive Clare Sullivan said the impacts of the change would be profound. “Instead of having one or two years from the diagnosis, they can have many, many more years of time with their loved ones,” she said. But she said the NDIS support packages were insufficient in meeting the needs of patients.

Advertisement

Advertisement

Lynch is determined to spend as much time as she can with her four “beautiful” grandchildren, and despite the overwhelming odds stacked against her, draws strength from the steadfast belief that MND will not win. “I’ve always said I’ll be the first person in the world to beat it. That’s my goal.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights. Sign up for our Morning Edition newsletter.

title: Cap Raise Crucible: Canaccord leads big mining dash for cash
text:
Advertisement

Sponsored BusinessCompaniesBulls N' Bears Cap Raise Crucible: Canaccord leads big mining dash for cash Brought to you by BULLS N’ BEARS Murray Ward September 11, 2026 — 1:02pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

This edition of Cap Raise Crucible dives into the ASX mining cash stampede as fat cheque books remain open for the exploration end of town. If anyone wondered whether the big cheque books were still open or not, the final week of August and opening days of September provided a fairly emphatic answer. Across a snapshot of 35 capital raisings examined by the Bulls N Bears Cap Raise Crucible, committed or targeted funds totalled $687.5 million, as companies went hunting for everything from mine development and acquisitions to money for drilling, commercialisation and plain old working capital slash “directors’ fees”. And nobody appeared to be working the phones harder than Canaccord Genuity. The investment bank turned up on nine mandates in our snapshot worth about $380 million in capital. Euroz Hartleys was next with five mandates and $328 million, while Argonaut Securities took out third spot with three and a not insignificant $211 million.

Advertisement

There is plenty of overlap in the dollar values because brokers frequently shared mandates, but the transaction count is harder to argue with. Nine. Five. Three. The broking desks were humming. But having your name on the most tombstones only wins one part of the contest. As always with the Bulls N Bears Cap Raise Crucible, the more interesting questions are what companies had to give away to get the money and whether investors were still smiling once the bookbuild champagne had gone flat. Three deals provided particularly useful answers.

Advertisement

FireFly Metals’ 1.464 million tonne copper equivalent Green Bay copper-gold project in Newfoundland, Canada. FIREFLY METALS (ASX: FFM) Funding package: $190 million Price: $1.78 Discount: 5.3 per cent

Advertisement

Current price: $1.81 – up 1.7 per cent FireFly Metals didn’t so much knock on the capital market’s door as walk through it carrying a wheelbarrow. The copper-gold developer assembled the period’s biggest funding package, comprising a $150 million Australian institutional placement, a Canadian-supplied war chest worth almost $30 million and a non-underwritten share purchase program (SPP) targeting another $10 million. The SPP is still to be completed. The new cash pile will help push FireFly’s 1.464 million tonne copper equivalent Green Bay copper-gold project in Newfoundland towards development. The funding is slated for underground works, drilling, infrastructure, long-lead items and feasibility studies, with the company assessing both a 1.8 million tonne-per-annum (Mtpa) base case and a larger 4.6Mtpa alternative. Canaccord Genuity Australia was sole lead manager and bookrunner to the Australian placement, with Euroz Hartleys and Argonaut Securities riding shotgun as co-managers.

Advertisement

A syndicate led by BMO Nesbitt Burns as lead underwriter and sole bookrunner, alongside RBC Dominion Securities, CIBC World Markets and Canaccord Genuity Corp., separately underwrote the Canadian portion of the raising. FireFly finished our 10th September pricing cut-off at $1.76, leaving the new money with its nose just below water. For the biggest funding package of the fortnight, that’s not a bad opening act given the small discount. PC GOLD (ASX: PC2) Equity raised: $77 million

Advertisement

Price: $1.05 Discount: 7.9 per cent Current price: $1.06– up one per cent PC Gold didn’t need FireFly-sized pockets to make its point. The company secured $75 million from institutional investors. Its incoming directors also put their hands in their pockets for another $2 million, with both sources kicking in at $1.05 per share, a 7.9 per cent discount to the previous close and a 5.4 per cent discount to the five-day volume-weighted average price (VWAP). Wallabi Group acted as joint lead manager and sole bookrunner, with Hannam & Partners and Canaccord Genuity Australia (again) also joint lead managers.

Advertisement

The money gives PC Gold considerable firepower at its Spring Hill project in the Northern Territory’s Pine Creek gold province, where a July resource update delivered 1.51 million ounces at 1.1 grams per tonne (g/t), including one million ounces in the indicated category. Funds will support a major drilling campaign, feasibility work and underground infrastructure as PC Gold chases resource growth and a higher-grade underground opportunity. At $1.09 as at our 9th September cut-off date, punters were just one per cent in front, but hey, a win is a win. A big cheque, a single-digit discount and an aftermarket price above issue is the kind of raising that gets everyone leaving the room claiming a victory of sorts. EUREKA GROUP HOLDINGS (ASX: EGH)

Advertisement

Equity raised: $80.2 million Price: 61.5 cents Premium: 0.8 per cent Current price: 64 cents – up 4.1 per cent There is nothing quite like a capital raise done at a premium to market to get a stock moving north. Eureka Group nailed both a premium and a resultant market price lift after putting away $80m in our snapshot period.

Advertisement

The affordable rental accommodation operator launched a fully underwritten $80.2 million accelerated entitlement offer at 61.5 cents – slightly above its 61-cent pre-halt close and just 0.4 per cent below its five-day VWAP. The money is helping fund the company’s $123.8 million acquisition of the NSW Living Portfolio, delivering a refreshing industry change and some M&A rather than just another drill program. MA Moelis Australia Advisory, Morgans Corporate and Unified Capital Partners were bookrunners, underwriters and joint lead managers. And institutions didn’t blink. The institutional component raised $70.7 million, with eligible institutional shareholders taking up 95.1 per cent of their entitlements. The remaining retail component is expected to raise $9.5 million.

Advertisement

Eureka closed at 64 cents on 9th September – 4.1 per cent above the offer price. Paying above the last trade for new stock and still making money isn’t normally how the discount game works. Together, the headline trio accounted for $347.2 million, or just over half the money chased during the entire snapshot window. For the right stories, the equity window wasn’t merely open. Somebody had taken the hinges off. Not everyone received quite the same treatment though. Broken Hill Mines’ high-grade silver-lead-zinc Pinnacles mine located 15 kilometres southwest of Broken Hill,NSW.

Advertisement

Broken Hill Mines secured a fully underwritten $90 million package at 76 cents, a 10.1 per cent discount, to fund production growth, drilling and infrastructure at its 4.8Mt at 9.2 per cent zinc equivalent Centenary project in NSW and its 6Mt running 10.9 per cent zinc equivalent Pinnacles project just next door. Petra Capital was sole lead manager, bookrunner and underwriter, with Euroz Hartleys as co-lead manager, Blue Ocean Equities as co-manager and Peloton Capital acting as broker to the placement. At 68 cents by our cut-off date, however, investors were 10.5 per cent underwater - the same open equity window, but a slightly different view from the other side. Andean Silver raised $40 million at $2.45 to accelerate work towards a potential restart of its Cerro Bayo silver-gold asset in Chile. Canaccord and Euroz were joint lead managers and bookrunners, with Jett Capital Advisors as co-manager. The 13.7 per cent discount looked generous. The stock sat at $2.30 by our cut-off date, so everybody’s 6 per cent on the wrong side of the ledger. Falcon Metals raised $30 million at 60 cents for drilling at its Blue Moon and Errabiddy gold projects, with Canaccord, Jett and Bell Potter splitting the clip. The 11.8 per cent discount price didn’t quite hold, with the stock now at 54 cents and investors 10 per cent in the hole.

Advertisement

Then things got more interesting. Titomic raised $16.5 million at 13 cents for its US expansion and commercialisation push, with Canaccord and Peloton as joint lead managers and Bell Potter weighing in as co-manager. The brokers held Titomic’s feet to the flames and extracted a hefty 23.5 per cent discount but were rewarded when the shares reached 14.5 cents, up 11.5 per cent, but you had to be quick. It was chocolates to boiled lollies in the end, with the stock at 12.5 cents at Sept 10 cut-off date. Sierra Nevada Gold raised $12.85 million at 10 cents for drilling at its As Safra copper-gold project in Saudi Arabia, with Fosters Stockbroking and Argonaut pulling the punters together. At 14 cents, investors were already up a whopping 40 per cent. Nice work if you can get it! Black Bear Minerals secured $12.5 million at 55 cents, with Canaccord as sole lead manager and bookrunner, to advance its Shafter silver project in Texas. At 54 cents, the new money was just a touch underwater.

Advertisement

The small cap punters that regularly swing off the coat tails of CPS Capital overran the $3.5m West Coast Silver raise that quickly turned into a $6 million raise at 9.5 cents at a 13.8 per cent discount. Paul Cronin, who achieved superman status along with Eric DeMori when the pair listed and grew Adriatic Metals to about $1.8 billion, weighed in as a cornerstone on this one. CPS has been sweet on West Coast Silver ever since raising its initial bag of cash at close to 3 cents, and while 9.5 cents now looks like a big win, those that chose not to sell at the heady price of 29 cents in December last year probably don’t think so. The stock has come off a little post-raise but will accelerate work at the historic Elizabeth Hill silver project in WA that has some of the highest-grade silver occurrences on the planet. The discount rack got considerably busier further down the list. Core Energy Minerals raised $3.025 million at 0.6 cents – a 25 per cent discount to market – for exploration at its Nova uranium joint venture in Namibia.

Advertisement

Canaccord was lead manager, earning a six per cent cash fee and, subject to approvals, a lazy 25 million broker options. At 0.7 cents, the new money was sitting on a sweet 16.6 per cent gain. Castle Minerals went the other way, raising $4 million at 7.5 cents with Euroz as lead manager – only 2.6 per cent below its previous close and actually a 4.7 per cent premium to its 15-day VWAP – principally for its Nielle gold project in Côte d’Ivoire. The new money has its nose in front with the stock sitting at eight cents. Critical Resources raised $1.6 million at half a cent, including $475,000 from directors, to fund exploration across its NZ, Canadian and Aussie projects along with its battery tech. 62 Capital got the gig as lead manager for a six per cent fee and a sweet 24 million broker options. At 0.7 cents, placement investors were a whopping 40 per cent ahead. Mount Ridley Mines raised $2 million at 3.3 cents plus a $100,000 director commitment to advance its Grass Patch rare earths project and its Selectro processing technology. Alpine Capital led the raise at an eye-catching 17.5 per cent discount, with the new shares streaking as high as 5.4 cents and closing on our cut-off date at 4.2 cents, a satisfying 27 per cent hike.

Advertisement

Jameson Resources raised $5 million at 3.5 cents, with PAC Partners acting as lead manager and bookrunner. Its ticker is currently trading at 3.8 cents, so punters are generally happy. Alliance Aviation Services raised $40 million at 70 cents for working capital and debt reduction, with Barrenjoey Markets underwriting the raise. It is currently trading at 59.5 cents - ouch! - while 4DS Memory sought almost $5 million at one cent alongside its proposed Jenesys acquisition, an Australian software developer specialising in Edge-AI (artificial intelligence processed locally on a device rather than in the cloud, with Jason Skinner’s JP Equity Holdings as lead manager. Punters are on the fence with the company trading at the offer price. Not every company required a broker to go rattling the tin. Duxton Farms’ $9.74 million raising involved an entitlement offer of one convertible note for every 11 shares, paying 7.5 per cent a year. Prescient Therapeutics went directly to shareholders too through a $7 million SPP, while WIN Metals raised $860,000 through notes paying 10 per cent. The IPO market, with three new entrants, added another layer.

Advertisement

Almasar Minerals raised $12 million at 20 cents, with Oracle Capital Group and 708 Capital as joint lead managers. The newcomer traded as high as 28 cents before closing at 22.5 cents on September 10, leaving subscribers 12.5 per cent ahead. Axiant Resources raised $8 million in its IPO at 20 cents with Argonaut as lead manager and bookrunner. It traded as high as 23.5 cents before closing at 19 cents, putting subscribers close to break-even. Powerhaus Uranium floated at 20 cents, with Canaccord and Pamplona Capital as joint lead managers to put away $9.5m. Its September 10 close of 23 cents handed thrill-seekers a 15 per cent gain. Three new floats. Three pretty comfortable starts. While some established companies had to reach deep into the discount rack to fill their books, the new kids wasted little time showing some of the old hands how it was done.

Advertisement

And that brings us back to the brokers and, in summary: Canaccord emerged as the busiest house with nine mandates, ahead of Euroz on five and Argonaut on three in our snapshot. Those dollar figures overlap; FireFly alone appears in all three, so the mandate count remains the cleaner scoreboard. For the brokers, the old soft-shoe shuffle remained the same – find enough of a discount to make institutional clients reach for their cheque books while persuading company boards they haven’t just sold the family silver. But this last fortnight once again showed why the bookbuild isn’t the final scoreboard. Broken Hill and Alliance Aviation’s new investors were underwater. Sierra Nevada’s were up a third. Mount Ridley and Critical Resources were both up more than 30 per cent -nice. Eureka asked institutions to pay slightly more than the stock’s last trade, attracted a 95.1 per cent institutional take-up and then closed above the offer price.

Advertisement

And the new kids supplied their own lesson: Powerhaus was 15 per cent above issue, Almasar 12.5 per cent, with Axiant treading water as at the 10th of September. Thirty-five deals and $687.5 million later, there was little evidence the Australian equity market had lost its mojo. However, plenty of evidence proved appetite can come at wildly different prices. For companies, getting cash in the tin matters and for brokers, getting the book away matters. For investors, only one thing really counts – what happened after they wrote the cheque. NationalWAHomelessness ‘Where else are they supposed to go?’ Two-day deadline to clear Perth homeless camp sparks fierce backlash Carla Hildebrandt September 11, 2026 — 1:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Five people sleeping rough in Perth’s southern suburbs have been given two days to pack up their personal belongings and move on, sparking backlash on social media. The City of Rockingham notice, issued by the team leader of ranger services on Wednesday, gives the five people camping at Baldivis wetlands until midday on Friday to remove their belongings. The Baldvis wetlands is about 45 kilometres south of Perth. Trails WA/T Lindsey According to the notice, anything left behind would be “removed and impounded” and held for between three days to two months, before they would be “destroyed”. The notice does say why the people are being moved on, or offer any assistance, only that it is in accordance with the Local Government Act.

Advertisement

But Homeless in Perth WA’s Facebook page administrator, Vangy Baker, who is in touch with the people living at the wetlands, said the people who were issued the notice have no car to move their items. The notice issued to homeless people sleeping at the Baldivis wetlands. “Moving tents and belongings does not resolve homelessness. It simply moves people from one patch of land to another,” Baker said. “If smaller, isolated camps around Baldivis, Rockingham or anywhere else are cleared without appropriate alternative accommodation, there is a real risk that more people will gather at visible locations. “Where else are they supposed to go?” Vangy Baker

Advertisement

The small camp at Baldvis is separate to a larger well-known homeless camp in Safety Bay along Memorial Drive, where roughly 150 homeless people are living in tents and their cars. Baker said she was contacted several times daily by “desperate” people in Perth who have nowhere to stay. “They are exhausted and frightened. Many services don’t have beds available, and they are repeatedly calling services that are already full,” she said. “People are being punished for being visible, while the fundamental problem remains unchanged - they have nowhere lawful and safe to sleep. “At an absolute minimum, there should be lawful safe parking and temporary sleeping areas near tilers and showers and other safe facilities.”

Shelter WA chief executive Kath Snell. Shelter WA Kath Snell, the chief executive of Shelter WA, the peak body for ending homelessness, said this was another example of how the state needed “urgent housing solutions”. “Moving people on doesn’t end homelessness, it just relocates it, and that is why Rockingham desperately needs more safe, secure, affordable homes, as well as a dedicated respite service for people doing it tough,” Snell said. “This is sadly yet another example of how dire our housing crisis is and how urgent we need housing solutions, both respite and long-term.” The notice has drawn hundreds of reactions and emotional comments on social media.

One person said it was the most “bloody appalling thing I’ve seen all year”. Others wanted to know why the notice had been issued in the first place.
