title: Superannuation is too important for populism
text:
Advertisement

September 11, 2026 — 12:44pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Australian workers have amassed an impressive pile of retirement savings. The nation’s superannuation pool has reached $4.8 trillion and is forecast to hit $8 trillion by the end of this decade. One Nation’s Barnaby Joyce and Pauline Hanson promote their proposed changes to the superannuation system. Alex Ellinghausen Since its introduction in the early 1990s, compulsory super has become a cornerstone of Australia’s economic architecture. Most Australians view it as an essential pillar of financial security in retirement. But as the pool grows, the politics of superannuation is becoming increasingly contested. This week, One Nation proposed a radical change to the retirement savings system; under its plan, those who rent or pay a mortgage would be able to take a quarter of their compulsory super contributions as take-home pay for up to three years.

Advertisement

One Nation leader Pauline Hanson claimed this would “give people some breathing room” to deal with persistent cost-of-living pressures. The proposal has been roundly criticised – and rightly so. If implemented, it would stoke inflation, perhaps Australia’s biggest economic challenge right now, and put upward pressure on interest rates. Rather than alleviating the cost-of-living crunch, One Nation’s super policy would worsen it. But it would also cause long-term damage by reducing retirement incomes. The Herald’s senior economics correspondent, Shane Wright, observed earlier this week that One Nation’s policy “confirms that superannuation is fast becoming the magic pudding of Australian politics, that it can do anything and everything”. At the past two federal elections, the Coalition has promised to change super rules so that aspiring home buyers could withdraw a portion of their superannuation and put it towards a deposit.

Advertisement

Economists criticised the Coalition’s plan, warning it would stoke demand for housing and push up prices, making the policy counterproductive. Even so, Liberal leader Angus Taylor has indicated an “open mind” to pursuing the scheme again, though the party is yet to announce a position. Related Article Opinion

Discrimination Early access to super benefits one group. You’re probably not a part of it Millie Muroi Economics Writer While Labor likes to style itself as the defender of the superannuation system, it has long encouraged super funds to invest in some of the “big national projects” that it favours, such as renewable energy and housing. But the nation’s retirement savings pool is not a political piggy bank. While populist superannuation policies must be resisted, that is not to say retirement savings policy should not be debated. It is not a sacred cow. Compulsory contributions were 3 per cent when the current superannuation system began in 1992, rising to 9 per cent by 2002 and 10 per cent by 2022. Now every Australian worker contributes a minimum of 12 per cent of their pay packet to super. It is entirely legitimate to examine whether that level is appropriate.

Advertisement

Public debate about superannuation rules often focuses on the concerns of middle- and high-income earners, but super policy must always serve the needs of low-income workers as well, especially women who still have lower average super balances than men. Australia’s superannuation pool is an invaluable national asset. Even small adjustments to the system should be made with great caution and only after careful consideration. Property sellers are increasingly moving away from the traditional auction in response to a softening housing market, new data from Domain suggests, with experts arguing that Australia has firmly entered a "buyer's market".

The online property platform has found a sharp rise in listings initially slated for auction being converted to private treaty in capital cities. Across Sydney, Melbourne, Brisbane, Adelaide and Canberra, the average proportion sales that are auctions has more than doubled from 29.6 per cent in February to 60.8 per cent in July.

Listings starting as private treaty also increased at the same time, highlighting a substantial move away from reliance on auction-day results as sellers seek the best price for their asset.

Domain's chief of economics and research, Nicola Powell, told SBS News that this shift in seller behaviour reflects the softening market conditions "unravelling across the nation".

"Many sellers are testing the market and realising that there just isn't that buyer depth there anymore," she said.

After major post-pandemic growth and following decades of steady increases, the Australian property market has seen a broad downturn over winter.

Data from property analyst Cotality shows that, while Sydney and Melbourne began to slow at the start of the year, national house price values peaked in March and have declined 3.6 per cent since.

Powell argued spring will likely be slower than usual, with Domain predicting property prices will continue to fall through the rest of the year.

"I think what we're going to see from buyers is they are going to want to get that greater value for money," she said.

The second quarter of 2026 saw the first sustained decline in national housing stock value since 2022, with Australian Bureau of Statistics figures showing a 0.3 per cent drop or $34.1 billion.

Auctions still a good idea

Shannan Whitney, co-founder of prominent Sydney property group BresicWhitney, told SBS News that shying away from auction sales could be the wrong move for sellers.

"Pricing tends to be more in line with where the market needs to be in an auction process than it does in a for sale process," he said.

"I think more vendors will be more comfortable with auction in Sydney over the next three or four months, but it just takes a little bit of time for everyone to work through the cycle."

Whitney expects the property cycle is now through its "first third" after months of price adjustments. It's "natural", he said, for sellers to want to retreat into non-auction sales where they feel safer or more in control during such a period, which he believes is now levelling off in Sydney.

"Vendors genuinely contemplating a sale are now much more aligned and educated about where the market is," he said. "Therefore, we think we expect to see clearance rates probably go up and improve over the next four months."

Sellers who aren't "in line" with the market should consider their position and perhaps pause on a sale for the next 12 months to three years, Whitney advised.

Buyers, on the other hand, are experiencing very favourable conditions. However, Whitney suggested that waiting and expecting prices to continue to drop might not be the best strategy.

Even though the market was soft, trading was better now compared with earlier in the year.

"What we're seeing now is much more engagement from buyers where they see pricing at reasonable, viable levels," he said. "We are seeing properties sell quicker now than we did six months ago."

Rapid corrections

Sustained high borrowing costs and stubborn inflation are some of the key drivers squeezing buyer affordability. At the same time, the surge in listings through autumn and winter forced national average clearance rates down to around 46 per cent.

"Listings have risen, choice is better than it once was, and particularly in markets like Sydney and Melbourne, it is very much a buyer's market," Powell said.

Economists note clearance rates below 60 per cent reduce inflationary pressure on house prices.

Major financial institutions including Commonwealth Bank have forecast a peak-to-trough decline in house prices of 8 to 10 per cent, with the market expected to hit its bottom in early 2027.

Those in the market are already pricing in the changed conditions, Whitney said, noting that the speed of information transfer at present means adjustments and property cycles happen far more quickly than they used to.

The Reserve Bank of Australia is widely expected to raise interest rates for the fourth time this year during its meeting at the end of this month. With an increased cash rate of 4.6 per cent, buyer confidence is expected to take a further hit.

If the RBA does increase rates this month, it is likely to trigger a continued "drag on inventory" as conditions slow even further.

"The cycle for buyers will lengthen and look more favourable," Whitney said.

title: 'Disfiguring': Behind the growing spread of a flesh-eating ulcer
text: In brief Buruli ulcer cases have spread beyond coastal Victoria, with new clusters reported in Melbourne suburbs. Researching are racing to find new ways to prevent the spread. Warmer weather has arrived, and mosquitoes will be buzzing about before you know it. As El Niño is expected to bring an early start to summer heat, it’s likely mosquitoes will make their presence felt earlier than usual. The threat of mosquitoes depositing flesh-eating bacteria has been restricted to a few parts of the country. But while rare, research shows it is now showing up in more areas — including in backyards in Melbourne’s inner city. So what exactly is Buruli ulcer, where is it now found, and how can you prevent it? Here’s what we know so far, and what researchers are currently developing to protect against the bacteria in future. What are Buruli ulcers? Buruli ulcer is a skin infection resulting from the bacterium Mycobacterium ulcerans. News that makes sense Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox. Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS. It starts as small and often painless inflammation after a mosquito bite, which may not be seen until months after initial infection. It transforms into a disfiguring ulcer after many weeks. If left untreated, it can continue increasing in size with a loss of skin and muscle. A buruli ulcer is treated with an eight-week course of antibiotics. Recovery can be much slower than expected for other common skin infections, with healing time highly dependent on the condition of the ulcer when first treated. It may take more than four months for ulcers to heal. How do people become infected? Mycobacterium ulcerans can infect urban wildlife, such as possums, which suffer symptoms similar to those in humans. Recent research has shown mosquitoes pass the bacterium to people. The mosquito most closely associated with areas at risk of Mycobacterium ulcerans is Aedes notoscriptus. Commonly known as the Australian backyard mosquito, it is widespread in Australia and commonly found in water-holding containers in suburban areas. There may be other pathways of infection, but health authorities have strongly encouraged people to prevent mosquito bites as the best way to avoid Buruli ulcer. Where is it found? Buruli ulcer has been reported in more than 30 countries around the world, including in Africa, South America and the Western Pacific. In Australia, it has been reported in several states, territories and regions, including Victoria, Far North Queensland, the Northern Territory and New South Wales. Victoria has been hit hardest, with 426 cases reported in the state in 2025 alone. Victorian cases have mostly been reported from coastal regions, but Melbourne’s suburbs have also seen an increase in activity. Inner north-west suburbs such as Essendon, Brunswick West and Moonee Ponds are part of the new cluster. With the potential for more cases, and in more locations, surveillance beyond known areas of activity is needed. Since Buruli ulcer became a notifiable disease in NSW, there have been six cases reported from the NSW south coast. There was concern this was because the Victorian outbreak had spread to the state and could also spread to new regions. But genomic analysis suggests the NSW cases are from a separate outbreak rather than spread from Victoria. This raises questions about how widespread this pathogen may be and what conditions are likely to give rise to human infections in new regions. How best to stop the flesh-eating bacteria’s spread? Australian health authorities have recommended insect repellents and reducing exposure to mosquitoes for decades to reduce the risks of mosquito-borne disease. But while health authorities might ordinarily consider insecticides to control mosquito populations, they’re not likely to be an effective way to reduce numbers of mosquitoes buzzing about the local suburbs in the long term. New research in Victoria led by two of us (Véronique Paris and Andrew Buultjens) tested a novel approach to mosquito control and found evidence that reducing mosquito numbers can also reduce a person’s risk of contracting Buruli ulcer. Using mosquitoes as pest-controllers Special devices, known as autodissemination stations, are designed to offer a breeding site to mosquitoes looking for somewhere to lay their eggs. A stinky mix of water and yeast draws them in. Once inside, the mosquito is exposed to a gauze strip coated with the control agent pyriproxyfen (an insect growth regulator) and Beauveria bassiana (insect specific fungus). When the mosquito leaves the station, its days are numbered due to the fungal infection. But before they die, they’ll transfer the mosquito control agent to other water-holding containers as they look for other places to lay their eggs. The mosquitoes become accidental pest controllers themselves. How effective was it? After eight weeks of station deployment, mosquito egg counts (a measure of mosquito activity) were 70% lower in treatment areas compared with control areas. Buruli ulcer presents an unusual challenge when trying to measure whether an intervention had impact on human disease because symptoms typically develop almost five months after infection. To account for this delay, we had to work backwards to estimate when infection likely occurred and use forensic genomic analysis to determine which cases were acquired locally. At the predicted peak of the mosquito-control effect, Buruli ulcer incidence was estimated to be 83 per cent lower in the treatment areas than in the control areas. The greater the reduction in mosquitoes, the greater the apparent protection from Buruli ulcer, providing further evidence that mosquito control can reduce disease risk. The mosquito control stations used in the study are not yet available for purchase in Australia, but regulatory approval for their use is imminent, and new products using similar approaches are also being tested. However, in this study the control stations were deployed in high numbers, so it’s unclear what the impact of their use in a single household would be. So how can you reduce your risk of Buruli ulcer this summer? Current predictions are for hot and relatively dry conditions this summer in eastern Australia. While this may mean there are fewer mosquitoes emerging from wetlands and other bodies of water, the mosquitoes closely associated with Mycobacterium ulcerans spread are found in our backyards. Water will still be available for mosquitoes around the home in bird baths, rainwater tanks, blocked drains, sump pits and roof gutters, and water left out for wildlife. To prevent mosquitoes from breeding in them, make sure you refill bird baths weekly, clear your gutters, cover water tanks, and empty and refill water for wildlife at least once per week. It’s also a good idea to keep using insect repellents. Mosquito control, whatever form it takes, will never get rid of all the mosquitoes. Covering up with long-sleeve shirts, long pants and enclosed shoes when outdoors will also help stop the bites. title: Aged care giant refunds $200,000 to residents over disputed living fees
text:
IN BRIEF Aged care provider Opal Healthcare has been forced to refund and credit almost $200,000 to its residents.

The government has introduced reforms to curb aged care providers' misuse of the Higher Everyday Living Fee.

One of Australia's largest aged care providers has been forced to refund almost $200,000 to residents after regulatory action from the Aged Care Quality and Safety Commission.

The provider, which SBS News can reveal is Opal Healthcare, refunded and credited almost 350 aged care residents following the commission's review of its Higher Everyday Living Fee (HELF) arrangements.

HELF was introduced by the Australian government in November. It is an optional fee Australians in residential aged care can pay for a higher standard of everyday lifestyle and food and beverage service.

SBS understands that the commission has found examples from a number of providers in addition to Opal for products that take advantage of the scheme.

These services, which have been reported by Australian media and have not been tied to Opal, include bundling services of Foxtel, newspapers, and wifi in a package for a resident who couldn't read, and charging residents to attend a volunteer choir that was coming to the aged care residential home.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

The commission's review also forced Opal Healthcare to reform charging practices and agreements and restore or provide services it had been charging residents for, at no additional fee.

"Our regulatory and complaints work is focused on protecting residents, ensuring the standard service offer meets the requirements of residents and ensuring providers meet their obligations," commissioner Liz Hefren-Webb said.

She said providers must take "proactive steps" to ensure those impacted "receive appropriate remediation".

Opal Healthcare manages 148 residential aged care facilities across Australia, which are home to more than 13,000 residents.

A spokesperson for the aged provider said that following Opal Healthcare's introduction of the HELF program in February, there were changes to the program guidelines.

"As a result, we identified that charges to approximately 2 per cent of residents required reversal to comply with the updated guidelines. We voluntarily reversed the relevant fees for all affected residents," the spokesperson told SBS News in a statement.

The spokesperson said the service "notified the regulator" in March and "ensured the correct billing" of all residents.

In a statement to SBS News, Hefren-Webb said her office has "seen examples" of providers requiring residents to pay for services that "should already be included as part of standard residential aged care, charging for services residents cannot or do not use, or presenting optional fees as though they are mandatory".

"We expect all providers to ensure fees are charged in accordance with the rules and their obligations, and that residents understand what they are paying for," she said.

"While we won't speculate on whether further refunds may occur elsewhere, the Commission will continue to scrutinise providers' practices and take action where necessary to protect older people."

Hefren-Webb said providers with a "willingness to cooperate and undertake early remediation" would be considered when deciding disciplinary action, but this would "not prevent regulatory action where the circumstances warrant it".

“Providers that identify a problem should act immediately to prevent any further impact on residents, notify the Commission, and commence remediation without delay."

The commission's action comes as the government implement aged care reforms that would stop providers from charging residents HELF for services they'd previously received for free before November 2025.

"We've always said it was unreasonable for providers to start charging older Australians for services they previously received at no cost," Aged Care Minister Sam Rae said in a statement on Thursday.

"We've listened to older people and we are acting now to make the rules clear and strengthen protections for older Australians."

He said the government has made it "very clear" that HELF is not for services that are part of "everyday care".

"It's common sense that services a provider was already delivering continue to be provided at no additional cost."

The reform follows the package of consumer protections delivered by the government earlier this year, including the commission's power to order refunds from services that are not fulfilling their obligations.

title: Want to reduce your dementia risk? Lifestyle changes are only part of the picture
text:
IN BRIEF New research has found social and environmental dementia risk factors are largely ignored in prevention strategies.

It's estimated that by 2065, more than one million Australians will be living with dementia.

Exercise, healthy eating and blood pressure management are the most common pieces of advice for those at risk of dementia. But new research suggests Australia is ignoring crucial factors.

Dr Jennifer Dunne, an epidemiologist who was the research lead on the Curtin University paper, said dementia prevention is focused heavily "on the individual".

She said the study, published in the peer-reviewed Lancet journal, was a "broader look" at dementia risk factors, mapping them to identify where "the evidence already was".

It builds off a "large systematic review and meta-analysis" previously conducted by co-author professor Blossom Stephan, Curtin's enAble Institute Dementia chair, which identified 61 risk factors — surpassing the previously identified 14.

The research, the first of its kind, categorised the 61 risk factors using a socioecological model.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

It found a lack of knowledge on how social and environmental conditions affect dementia — information crucial for dementia prevention.

Dunne, a Curtin University Dementia Centre of Excellence research fellow, said the report identifies "gaps" where researchers "should be looking".

"There's so much focus on preventing dementia, but we need to think more broadly about how we work together to prevent it," Dunne said.

"We need to move away from the message of telling people you need to do all these [lifestyle] things because they can only be successful if the environment around them is supportive."

Risk factors are 'all interlinked'

Dementia is an umbrella term for more than 100 conditions — the most common being vascular dementia and Alzheimer's disease.

Alzheimer's accounts for up to 80 per cent of dementia cases, and impacts a person's memory, thinking and behaviour.

Source: SBS News

Dementia is caused by neurodegeneration — damage or death of the brain's neurons.

Uncorrected vision or hearing loss, social isolation and early childhood education are among the study's 61 risk factors.

"You start thinking about dementia prevention in mid-life ... but you can't go back and do your childhood education again — you can't change that risk factor," Dunne explained.

"We need to ensure that the broader society in which we live supports high-quality education that is accessible to everybody."

She noted that employed adults face a higher risk of social isolation as they approach retirement age.

Social isolation is enmeshed with other risk factors including loss of vision, loss of hearing, physical inactivity and depression.

"We know that when people sometimes become socially isolated, they become depressed. Then they tend to withdraw and stop exercising. They might start smoking, or start smoking more, which leads to a cascade of health conditions. It's all interlinked," Dunne said.

Stephan said the research must be turned into "action".

"Dementia prevention should support healthy choices while also improving education, neighbourhoods, healthcare access and other social conditions that shape brain health across the population throughout a person's life," she said.

Dementia 'close' to a public health crisis

According to the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare, 439,000 Australians were living with dementia in 2025 — of those, 56 per cent are women.

A person's risk of dementia increases with age, with 42.7 per cent of Australians aged 90 and over living with the condition.

Currently, dementia is the leading cause of death in Australia.

It's estimated that more than one million Australians will have dementia by 2065.

Dunne said dementia is "already pretty close" to being a national public health crisis.

READ MORE Leader in dementia research shares four ways you can reduce your risk

One way to counter that is ensuring Australians are ageing well.

"The whole goal is to keep people healthy and make sure we live in environments that are supportive to us — and that the government have a lot they can do to prevent dementia," Dunne said.

Professor Tanya Buchanan, Dementia Australia CEO, said the research reaffirmed that "dementia risk reduction is a collective responsibility".

"It is vital everyone has access to the supports and services they need to support their brain health,” she said.

“Alongside addressing brain health behaviour at an individual level, we need policies and actions from governments and organisations to make it easier for everyone to lower their risk of dementia.”

title: Donald Trump's 'only condition' for $5,000 payments to every American
text:
In brief US President Donald Trump has promised to pay every American adult US$5,000 should Republicans win the midterms.

The promise came during a lengthy speech to supporters at the Republican midterm convention in Dallas, Texas.

President Donald Trump said on Thursday he would pay every US adult a US$5,000 ($6,926) "Trump dividend" if Republicans retain control of Congress in November's midterm election, an extraordinary attempt to persuade voters to back his party.

"If the Republicans win, you win with us, and you get $5,000. It will be called the Trump dividend," he told the Republican midterm convention audience in Dallas, Texas.

Trump likened the payments to a corporation's distributions to shareholders, citing "our tremendous strength and success economically".

He did not say where the money would come from — with the theoretical bill likely topping US$1.35 trillion ($1.85 trillion) — citing only that "our country is making so much money".

It was also unclear how the payments would work or whether they would be legal.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

The promise would require congressional approval, and would further exacerbate the country’s nearly US$1.8 trillion annual budget deficit and concerns about inflation.

The payment would also come with a catch — Trump was clear he only wanted US citizens spending their prospective windfalls at home.

"But the only condition on the payment of this dividend that we’re going to be making … is that it must be spent in the United States of America," Trump told the convention crowd.

"We don’t want you going to Canada to spend the money. We don't want you going to China, to Germany. We got to spend the money in the United States of America."

Trump did not say how he and his administration would ensure the funds were only spent in the US.

During a primetime address that lasted an hour and 45 minutes, Trump boasted of completing "the greatest two years in the history of the presidency", putting himself squarely at the centre of the election despite his deepening unpopularity.

But it was not clear whether his campaign-style speech would appeal to the critical swing voters who opinion polls show have drifted away from Trump's party, amid growing dissatisfaction with the cost of living and the war on Iran.

"We hand America's future to the radical left Democrats, and our nation will spend the next decade just getting back on its feet," he said. "Vote Republicans, and we will leave the world in our dust for generations to come."

Within an hour, vice president JD Vance appeared to try to walk back Trump’s proposal — at least in part — by suggesting the dividend payments would not go to the wealthy. Vance suggested it could be paid for by US tariff revenues, though the suggested payment dwarfs what the US has taken in through the protectionist measures.

The US Congress would need to approve or otherwise acquiesce to the payment. The sum would far exceed US tariff revenues even before the Supreme Court tossed much of the president’s tariff program last year.

The national debt last month topped US$40 trillion ($55 million) for the first time.

Trump has frequently lamented that, during the modern era, the sitting president's party almost always loses seats in Congress during the midterms, and he has looked for unorthodox ways to defy the trend, including this week's convention.

"We’re going to change that,” Trump said. “There’s no reason for it."

New Mexico-based lawyer John Day said Trump's proposal would have to be approved by Congress, but it would be legal because the payment would go to everyone regardless of how they voted, or whether they voted at all.

"This is a campaign promise," Day said. "It’s not a payment to individuals to try to get them to vote in a particular way."

In search of a 'Trumpapalooza' poll bump

The two-day Dallas gathering, where Trump will also deliver the closing remarks on Friday after Vance's keynote address, underscores the extent to which Republicans' fortunes are tethered to Trump and serves as a showcase for their strategy ahead of the 3 November midterm elections.

The event was so centred on Trump that Republican National Committee chairman Joe Gruters informally dubbed it "Trumpapalooza," a nod to the popular Lollapalooza music festival.

The focus on Trump amounts to a risky bet that he can mobilise the voters who carried him to the presidency two years ago, despite public polls showing his approval ratings have hit an all-time low. Trump vowed to pay multiple visits to battleground states and districts in the eight weeks until election day.

"I'm asking you to pretend that I'm on the ballot," Trump said, a line that may have pleased Democratic campaign strategists just as much as MAGA voters.

Though Trump insisted the 21,000-seat arena was "packed", the upper sections remained largely empty during his speech capping Thursday's program.

title: The countries showing Australia a way out of its 'miserable' classroom situation
text:
Heightened classroom disruption, gender divides, dwindling reading and maths scores — a major global student performance report shows Australian schools are continuing to slide backwards on key measures.

Every three years, the global Programme for International Student Assessment (PISA) measures student literacy in mathematics, reading, science and computational problem-solving.

The 2025 edition, which tested 15-year-olds from 91 OECD countries and economies, also measured the effects of gender divides, differences between high and low socio-economic status, and the impacts of technology and classroom disruption.

In the latest report, released on Tuesday, Australia's scores continued a 20-year decline, with maths and reading at Australia's lowest since testing began in 2000.

But Pasi Sahlberg, a Finnish education expert, author and professor at the University of Melbourne, says reports focusing on issues with the Australian school system were missing the big picture.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

"The headline is that we have all-time-low results. I think it's absolutely astonishing that our mainstream media are saying this. The truth is every country in the OECD is showing all-time-low results in everything. Very few countries were able to improve their results in 2025," Sahlberg told SBS News.

Australia's scores are on a 20-year decline, but that isn't the full story. Source: SBS News

In the global ranking, Australia moved up one place in reading to 11th, maintained its 17th place in maths, and fell one place in science to 11th. In the computational problem solving category, introduced in 2025, Australia ranked 8th globally. Australia's scores were well above the OECD average in all four key tests.

On Wednesday, in light of the results, federal Education Minister Jason Clare announced new reforms in reading, mathematics and science. He pointed to England's success — the country jumped three places in reading to reach the top 10, four places in maths to 10th place and seven places in science to rank at 8th in the 2025 PISA report — to illustrate a need for various reforms. This includes a focus on phonics, which is a method of teaching reading and writing that uses the sounds of spoken language, changes to the maths curriculum, and reforms to screen time.

"The UK results are impressive. It’s also hard-earned. It’s something almost 20 years in the making," Clare said in a statement.

He said that Australian schools that have been following English methods for a while are showing improvements but he wants a broader roll-out.

There has been a general decline in literacy across all OECD countries. Source: SBS News

'We are all in this miserable situation together'

But Sahlberg said Clare's reforms were the wrong response.

"We need to look beyond these rankings, because this data is also showing us a very alarming situation in Australia and many other countries when it comes to how young people experience learning in school."

Sahlberg said the issues affecting children's learning also occurred outside the classroom: parents are reading less and have less interest or engagement with their children's schooling.

The PISA report, which showed that 75 per cent of students in Australia reported that their parents or guardians asked them, at least once per week, what they did at school, down from 81 per cent in 2022.

"England, Canada, USA, all the others, we are all in this miserable situation together," when it comes to a decline in a positive culture around reading, he said.

What are countries with the highest scores doing that Australia isn't?

In the Asia-Pacific region, several Chinese regions, Singapore, Taiwan (which participates in PISA under the name Chinese Taipei), Macao and Japan took the top five PISA spots across mathematics, reading, science and computational problem-solving.

While Singapore and Japan's scores decreased slightly from the previous PISA ranking, Taiwan, China and Macao all saw slight increases in their scores, outliers across most participating OECD countries.

Australia's mathematics score remained steady in 2025. Source: SBS News

For Therese Keane, digital learning expert and professor in STEM Education in the School of Education at La Trobe University, the secret to Singapore's success was in its handling of technology in the classroom.

"Singapore is a great example of combining high technology with clear learning guidance, with subject-specific digital learning guidance in schools," she told SBS News.

Keane said that technology was ushered into Australian classrooms hastily during former prime minister Kevin Rudd's digital education revolution program. She said the quick move left the technology ubiquitous, without proper guidelines for use.

"Technology is important in the classroom, but it needs to be used with intention and guidelines," Keane said.

"I think we've got to be very careful that we don't throw the baby out with the bath water in terms of technology and AI because when you look at countries like Singapore, Estonia, the regions of China, PISA shows that the technologies do not automatically undermine the learning."

Estonia, a country with a strong focus on tech, nonetheless ranks highly in reading literacy. Source: SBS News

She said the difference is that technology is embedded within a strong system of teaching, curriculum, expectations and classroom management.

"These high performing countries that we're seeing, they're not anti-technology. And I want the message to be that they're much more willing to draw a hard line between, say, learning technology and personal technology."

But there are big cultural and structural differences at play, too. Sahlberg, who has worked in schools across Singapore, Japan and China, said that high PISA scores seen in those countries come at a "huge" social cost.

READ MORE Could AI in classrooms stop children falling behind at school?

"In these countries, about 80 to 100 per cent of kids go to school after daily school."

"They have their private lessons every evening, and then they go to school on Saturdays and often Sundays as well — this comes with a huge human cost, and social cost."

Sahlberg said that if Australia wanted to do something similar to those high-performing countries, then a question to ask would be, "how many parents would like to do that to their own children?"

Australia ranked equal tenth with New Zealand for science literacy. Source: SBS News

But, he said, the solution to Australia's problem was clear.

"We don't need to go to Singapore or England or Shanghai to see what they do; we have the solution in this country.

"Our politicians and system leaders should redesign the school architecture: We have 24 jurisdictions, and they don't share their best practices; they don't tell others what works in their systems because they are competing.

The countries and economies topping the PISA rankings all have a more centralised learning curriculum, but in Australia, there are vast differences between our state, Catholic and independent schools. Salhberg says supporting the current "highly competitive, fragmented, siloed education system that is incapable of learning from itself" was a waste of learning opportunities.

"How can we release this potential and good practice that we have in this country?" he asked.

"This is the lesson we should take from PISA."

title: Winner of Alone Season 4 plans to donate some of their $250,000 prize to a competitor
text:
in brief Former Navy chef Trent Fenton survived 52 freezing days to win Alone Australia season four.

Now back home, he plans to pay off his mortgage and support fellow competitors.

"It was a feeling that I'll cherish for the rest of my life."

Alone Australia season four has reached its icy conclusion with one man left standing in Finland's frozen north: Trent Fenton.

The 40-year-old former Navy chef told SBS News in his first post-show interview that re-watching the moment his wife Em tapped him on the shoulder to reveal he had made it still gets him.

"I started even choking up a little bit, which was weird because I'm not that kind of guy normally," Fenton said.

"That's why people love Alone. It's just pure emotion."

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

Season four of the hit survivalist show took participants away from Oceania and into the wilds of Sápmi, deep within the Arctic Circle. Dropped along the shore of lake Rahajärvi, they had to battle sub-zero temperatures, extreme calorie deficits, and total isolation for a chance to win $250,000.

Father-of-three Fenton spent 52 days alone, outlasting nine other contenders — who either gave up or were deemed medically unable to continue — but said he is "no amazing survivalist".

Asked what he plans to do with the prize, he says he plans to donate part of it to causes championed by some of his competitors and pay down his mortgage.

The final episode of the season saw the other remaining finalists — 57-year-old farmer Clint and 24-year-old permaculture educator Jasper — pushed to their limits.

After spending a night spent throwing up, Clint called time on his 48th day in the wilderness, saying, "there are things in life worth more than money — like health, love, companionship, friends and family".

"When you haven’t got them, you realise just how important they are.”

Just a day later, Jasper was medically extracted after an infection in his hand was found to be spreading. He said he was leaving the show "a new person" after being challenged in the extreme.

"These 48 days have been some of the best of my life," Jasper said. "I’m proud of how far I pushed myself and feel at peace knowing I’ve done the experience justice."

Perspective the key to survival

As a child, Fenton said he would "get into a bit of strife", which prompted his father to relocate the family from Hobart to the Tasmanian Midlands where he could "get my nose clean".

"Mate, I've never looked back. I love everything about the bush and hunting and fishing," he said. "It was really my element out there."

The well-honed skills needed to sustain himself on whatever he could catch or forage were backed by a "bucketload of resilience", which Fenton said he developed in the Navy.

Ten survivalists ventured into the remote Arctic wilderness of Sápmi, Finland, for Alone Australia season four. Credit: SBS

"I joined the Navy not knowing that I suffered severe seasickness," he said. "After four years throwing my guts up, I thought, 'If you can push through something like that, it puts you in good stead for most things that you're going to run into'."

Still, Fenton said he entered the competition with the mentality that it would be "the adventure of a lifetime" and that, even if he faced starvation, as many contestants do, he was always in the "privileged" position to be able to escape it — unlike many around the world, particularly those in Gaza.

All about the trout

The strategy which saw him take home $250,000 in prize money relied on bringing in as many fish as he could. While Finland was "a bit colder than good old Tassie", Fenton said as long as he had access to fish, he believed he would have a solid chance.

His commitment to fishing meant that, unusually for a contestant on Alone — which often sees people go for weeks without a solid meal — Fenton rarely struggled for food.

"One of the producers actually said to me, 'Trent, I've seen no one in the existence of Alone Australia put in as much time fishing or making stuff to fish as you did'," he said.

Temperatures in northern Finland can reach as low as negative 30C, with snow covering the ground from October through to April. Credit: SBS

Reliance on fishing, however, meant that the day he lost a prized, handmade lure which had secured him over 30 fish was a real blow.

"I was devastated," he said. "If you watch the last episode ... I had a full dummy spit, and I threw my rod, and I was swearing."

"If someone said to me, 'Mate, you give me your car at home and I'll give that lure back to you', I would have done it in a heartbeat."

'Dark days' in the final stretch

Even with his well-stocked bag of dried fish, Fenton said not knowing whether his competitors also had food meant never quite feeling secure and constantly wondering if he had enough to outlast them.

The "dark days" came just before his seven-week-plus finish when the lake began to freeze but the ice wasn't thick enough to walk on.

"I couldn't spear fish ... I couldn't go and forage any berries or mushrooms ... what do I actually do?" Fenton said. "I just thought, 'I don't really want to be here, this is rubbish, I'm just bored, I can't do anything'."

Little did he know, he was just hours away from seeing his wife again, something that Fenton said was challenging to re-adjust to.

"I wasn't ready to go home. I hadn't mentally prepared or even started checking out for that," he said.

"A couple of days after getting taken off the land, some weird things go through your mind, and I struggled to come to terms with a lot of them."

Memories and money

Now that he's back in his regular life, Fenton said he plans to pay off the mortgage, invest money for his children to use later in life, and start "creating memories" with his family.

He also plans to donate some of his winnings to fellow competitor and ex-serviceman Dylan Hyatt-Jacobson, who opened up about his family's struggles with IVF treatment during his time on the show.

Ultramarathon runner Sia Kindberg, who tapped out in episode six due to frostbite, is raising money for survivors of slavery, human trafficking, and abuse with a Sydney to Melbourne run in October. Fenton said he will be donating to her cause as well.

As the temperatures dropped, the fish Fenton relied on moved into deeper, warmer water, where he was unable to follow them across the thin ice. Credit: SBS

Incredibly, after 52 days, the Alone Australia season four winner said he may not be done just yet — and is keen to find out exactly where his breaking point is.

"All the other competitors ... they could either see that they were medically unfit, or they were literally physically checked out; they know where their breaking point is. Whereas I kind of didn't experience that," Fenton said.

"Hopefully there's another time where there's another season of Alone with all the winners or something like that.

"That would be another amazing experience just to try and have another crack."

title: How an NFL match in Melbourne came to be, and its historic links
text:
In brief The NFL will stage its first regular-season game in Australia, with the 49ers facing the Rams at the MCG.

The multi-year NFL deal, secured amid stiff interstate competition, has Melbourne preparing to host up to 100,000 fans.

Anticipation is building ahead of the NFL's big Australian debut.

The San Francisco 49ers take on the Los Angeles Rams at the Melbourne Cricket Ground on Friday morning in what will be the league's first regular-season game in Australia, and just the second game overall of the 2026 season.

The match kicks off on Friday at 10.35am and is geared around the Thursday night TV audience in the US. Kick-off time will be 5.35pm on the US West Coast and 8.35pm on the East Coast.

How did the NFL land in Victoria?

The NFL has a four-year contract with Victoria to host at least two games in Melbourne, with an option for a third, and is part of the NFL’s International Series, which started in 2007 at London's Wembley Stadium.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

The Victorian government beat out serious bids from both NSW and Western Australia to host these games, and is thought to be paying the NFL about $15 million per game.

How often does the NFL play outside the US?

The match at the MCG will be one of nine international matches scheduled this season — including matches in Paris, Rio de Janeiro, Munich, Madrid, and London. NFL commissioner Roger Goodell has expressed interest in having every team play once in a foreign market each season.

Games have also been staged in Germany, Brazil, Mexico and Canada before.

While exhibition games between NFL teams have been played beyond US borders since 1969, some countries, like England, took time to build a following, while others, like Mexico, embraced it immediately.

In fact, the largest crowd in NFL history is 112,376 at the Azteca Stadium in Mexico City in 1994 when the Houston Oilers beat the Dallas Cowboys.

Other stadiums have also hosted NFL regular-season games outside the United States, including the Bernabéu in Madrid, Croke Park in Dublin, Twickenham in London, plus stadiums in Berlin, Munich, Frankfurt and São Paulo in Brazil.

The NFL has ramped up international efforts in recent times by inviting teams to apply for international marketing rights for various countries.

Are both the teams in Australia already?

As of Wednesday afternoon, only one of the two teams playing on Friday — the San Francisco 49ers — has arrived in Australia.

"This has been such a cool experience," said 49ers running back Christian McCaffrey.

"There were question marks when we heard we were playing in Australia. Since we got here, it has been so cool. The people are unbelievable, the food's incredible, the coffee is great. The atmosphere, you can already feel it, it's been so much fun and we are super fired up we're here."

Four teams have been given the rights to Australia and New Zealand — the Los Angeles Rams, Philadelphia Eagles, Las Vegas Raiders, and the reigning Super Bowl champions, the Seattle Seahawks.

Therein lies one of the ironies of this week.

The Rams are one of Australia's designated teams — but they're not here until 24 hours before the game, electing to try to stay on US time to avoid jet lag — a fly-in, fly-out mission.

San Francisco 49ers head coach Kyle Shanahan says the team has acclimatised to the time difference after a 16-hour flight from the US. Source: AAP / Joel Carrett

The 49ers players have been taking in some of the sights and sounds of Melbourne, and winning a lot of local hearts in the process. Already one of the NFL's more popular teams, it's now even more likely there will be more 49ers fans than Rams fans among the expected 100,000 fans at the MCG on Friday.

Ironically, 49ers coach Kyle Shanahan was perhaps the loudest complainer when this game was scheduled earlier this year.

“Nothing against (Melbourne). It looks awesome. People seem really cool. Makes me want to come back and visit with my family," Shanahan told reporters.

"But we have 17 games. We play once a week, so we are all about business right now ... My message to the players was to enjoy their one day off, get hydrated and get used to the time difference. And we have done that."

A historical precedent

It's not the first time two US teams will take to the hallowed ground of the MCG — the first American football match played there was in 1908, between sailors of the USS Minnesota and the USS Kentucky.

In 1925, the US sent a 57-warship armada for a friendly visit to Australia and New Zealand, a post-war exercise in geopolitical and public relations designed to boost sailor morale while also building Pacific alliances in the face of growing Japanese aggression.

Forty-three of those ships would arrive in Melbourne to great public interest.

Records show that US sailors held boxing matches and played baseball at the MCG against some of the best Australian cricketers of the day. But it was a gridiron match between US sailors from the USS Trenton and USS Pennsylvania that caught Melbourne's attention.

At a muddy Punt Road Oval, a stone's throw from the MCG, sailors from the Pennsylvania beat the sailors from the Trenton in front of 3,000 people in a match that, according to the Royal Historical Society of Victoria, included VFL footballers.

In 1999, the Denver Broncos and San Diego Chargers played a pre-season exhibition match in Sydney in 1999. The match was played at Stadium Australia in Homebush in front of almost 74,000 fans. In the heart of rugby league country, its American mutation drew curiosity but failed to satisfy. The New York Times' John Shaw reported at the time that the crowd was "about 20,000 smaller" than the NFL had hoped for. Shaw reported that "canned applause was frequently blasted across the stadium when the audience was slow to cheer".

How to watch San Francisco 49ers vs Los Angeles Rams in Australia?

Kick off is at 10.35am for the eastern states and territories, 10.05am in SA and the NT, and 8.35am in WA.

Australians will be able to watch the match on Fox Sports and Kayo via a subscription, or on free-to-air on Seven or 7Plus. Coverage starts at 10am.

title: 'Absolute nightmare': Mass flight cancellations in the UK prompt calls for dismissals
text:
in brief A total of 1,055 flights to and from UK airports had been axed by 8pm (5am AEST) .

Ryanair COO Neal McMahon repeated his calls for NATS chief executive Martin Rolfe to be fired.

Consumer chaos has descended on the UK's busiest airports as an air traffic glitch causes major disruptions, prompting calls to fire the head of the air traffic control service.

Almost 1,100 flights to and from UK airports were cancelled Tuesday, due to what the country's air traffic control service called a technical issue, in this latest error.

A total of 1,055 flights to and from British airports had been axed by 8pm (5am AEST) according to the aircraft tracking website FlightRadar24.

"Recovery from today's system issue has taken longer than we had hoped," Britain's air traffic control service, known as NATS, said on social media.

"Our system issue is now resolved, we are operating normally and working as hard as possible to clear the backlog of flights," it noted, adding "this is hugely frustrating and apologise unreservedly".

Tuesday's issues follow a technical glitch in July last year that saw scores of flights to and from the UK cancelled and which prompted anger from airline chiefs.

Britain saw its worst air systems failure in years in 2023, with more than 700,000 passengers affected after hundreds of flights were delayed or cancelled.

'Absolute nightmare'

Heathrow Airport, Britain's largest and busiest airport, in west London, confirmed it was among those affected on Tuesday, along with Gatwick to the south of the UK capital.

"It's just an absolute nightmare down there," healthcare worker Josie Donoghue said of Gatwick after leaving the airport, having had to disembark her flight to Ireland after three hours stuck on the runway.

"Getting through that airport was like trying to get out of Alcatraz," she told Britain's domestic Press Association news agency.

Liverpool, Birmingham and Edinburgh airports were also affected, while Dublin Airport in Ireland said it had cancelled dozens of flights.

British Airways said it had to cancel or divert more than 100 flights, affecting tens of thousands of its customers.

Irish no-frills carrier Ryanair said more than 65,000 passengers had been disrupted and it had cancelled more than 50 flights.

Arsenal, due to play Napoli in the Champions League on Wednesday in the southern Italian city, were forced to cancel a press conference ahead of the match after the team's flight was delayed.

UK transport secretary Heidi Alexander said on X she was "seeking assurances that lessons will be learned and systems that support aviation are up to the job".

But Ryanair COO Neal McMahon repeated his calls for NATS chief executive Martin Rolfe to be fired, accusing him of having again "failed UK travellers".

"Enough is enough, it's time for the UK government to intervene ... and put somebody in charge who can do the job."

Over the past four decades, Nicole Lynch has watched motor neurone disease strip her family members of their agency and rob years from their lives. In 1995, her cousin was diagnosed with MND. Not long after, so was another cousin. Her mother died from MND at the age of 51, and her family suspects it killed both of her grandparents on her mother’s side too. Lynch will be one of the beneficiaries of the PBS listing of a new treatment for a rare form of ALS. James Brickwood “It’s awful … The worst thing about it is knowing what’s going to happen,” the 54-year-old said. Her family carries a gene mutation that causes amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS). While ALS is the most common form of MND – the same disease that killed AFL great Neale Daniher – only 2 per cent of people with MND will suffer from this particular mutation.

Advertisement

Related Article Health Bronte calls for her mum in the dark of night, scared of dying. There is no cure for her condition Lynch’s 25-year-old daughter carries the gene mutation. For the first time, patients with the rare form of MND will be able to access a new treatment on the PBS that could extend their lifespan by years. From October 1, Tofersen will be subsidised on the national scheme. Professor Dominic Rowe is a clinical neurologist who treats several patients with Tofersen. He said the treatment was able to change the progression of disease in people with SOD1-related MND. When SOD1 mutates, Rowe explains, it acquires what is known as a “toxic gain of function”.

Advertisement

This means the gene – which, in a body without MND, usually protects cells from damage – instead begins attacking and gradually destroying motor neurons in the brain and spine. “What the therapy does is reduce the amount of toxic protein in a patient’s motor neurons, and by reducing that toxic protein, improves the ability of motor neurons to survive, and slows the progression of their loss,” Rowe said. “When you slow the progression of motor neuron loss, you slow the progression of weakness, ultimately translating into improved quality of life and improved survival.” Lynch, who was diagnosed with MND in December 2021, travels from the mid-North Coast to Sydney every three weeks to receive the treatment she describes as “life-changing”. Her team administers local anaesthetic before injecting a dose of Tofersen via a lumbar puncture that sends the fluid directly into the central nervous system. Lynch spends the night in hospital recovering.

Advertisement

She started the treatment in March 2022, and said her deterioration had come to “a standstill”. A patient diagnosed with MND is expected, on average, to live just two years beyond their diagnosis. Lynch has survived almost five. “I see the treatment as my best friend,” she said. She walks with a limp due to muscular atrophy caused by the disease, so her left calf is much skinnier than her right. Between 35 and 40 per cent of MND patients experience their first symptoms in the lower limbs. Lynch fears, more than anything, how her loss of independence will burden her children in the future.

Advertisement

“Walking up and down stairs is extremely difficult,” she said. “Having to ask people for help, it sucks. It’s like, hang on, I’m the wife and the mother, I should be doing that … It’s the simple things. “I have really dark days. But I keep it to myself. I don’t like upsetting other people, I don’t want to be a burden.” Patients will now pay a maximum of $25 per script for Tofersen. Concession cardholders will pay just $7.70. Before the subsidy, it cost patients up to $28,600 per dose. It is the second treatment for MND listed on the PBS by the Albanese government, and the third overall.

Advertisement

“MND is a heartbreaking, insidious disease that Australians are all too familiar with,” Health Minister Mark Butler said on Friday. Health Minister Mark Butler. Dominic Lorrimer MND Australia chief executive Clare Sullivan said the impacts of the change would be profound. “Instead of having one or two years from the diagnosis, they can have many, many more years of time with their loved ones,” she said. But she said the NDIS support packages were insufficient in meeting the needs of patients.

Advertisement

Advertisement

Lynch is determined to spend as much time as she can with her four “beautiful” grandchildren, and despite the overwhelming odds stacked against her, draws strength from the steadfast belief that MND will not win. “I’ve always said I’ll be the first person in the world to beat it. That’s my goal.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights. Sign up for our Morning Edition newsletter.

title: Cap Raise Crucible: Canaccord leads big mining dash for cash
text:
Advertisement

Sponsored BusinessCompaniesBulls N' Bears Cap Raise Crucible: Canaccord leads big mining dash for cash Brought to you by BULLS N’ BEARS Murray Ward September 11, 2026 — 1:02pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

This edition of Cap Raise Crucible dives into the ASX mining cash stampede as fat cheque books remain open for the exploration end of town. If anyone wondered whether the big cheque books were still open or not, the final week of August and opening days of September provided a fairly emphatic answer. Across a snapshot of 35 capital raisings examined by the Bulls N Bears Cap Raise Crucible, committed or targeted funds totalled $687.5 million, as companies went hunting for everything from mine development and acquisitions to money for drilling, commercialisation and plain old working capital slash “directors’ fees”. And nobody appeared to be working the phones harder than Canaccord Genuity. The investment bank turned up on nine mandates in our snapshot worth about $380 million in capital. Euroz Hartleys was next with five mandates and $328 million, while Argonaut Securities took out third spot with three and a not insignificant $211 million.

Advertisement

There is plenty of overlap in the dollar values because brokers frequently shared mandates, but the transaction count is harder to argue with. Nine. Five. Three. The broking desks were humming. But having your name on the most tombstones only wins one part of the contest. As always with the Bulls N Bears Cap Raise Crucible, the more interesting questions are what companies had to give away to get the money and whether investors were still smiling once the bookbuild champagne had gone flat. Three deals provided particularly useful answers.

Advertisement

FireFly Metals’ 1.464 million tonne copper equivalent Green Bay copper-gold project in Newfoundland, Canada. FIREFLY METALS (ASX: FFM) Funding package: $190 million Price: $1.78 Discount: 5.3 per cent

Advertisement

Current price: $1.81 – up 1.7 per cent FireFly Metals didn’t so much knock on the capital market’s door as walk through it carrying a wheelbarrow. The copper-gold developer assembled the period’s biggest funding package, comprising a $150 million Australian institutional placement, a Canadian-supplied war chest worth almost $30 million and a non-underwritten share purchase program (SPP) targeting another $10 million. The SPP is still to be completed. The new cash pile will help push FireFly’s 1.464 million tonne copper equivalent Green Bay copper-gold project in Newfoundland towards development. The funding is slated for underground works, drilling, infrastructure, long-lead items and feasibility studies, with the company assessing both a 1.8 million tonne-per-annum (Mtpa) base case and a larger 4.6Mtpa alternative. Canaccord Genuity Australia was sole lead manager and bookrunner to the Australian placement, with Euroz Hartleys and Argonaut Securities riding shotgun as co-managers.

Advertisement

A syndicate led by BMO Nesbitt Burns as lead underwriter and sole bookrunner, alongside RBC Dominion Securities, CIBC World Markets and Canaccord Genuity Corp., separately underwrote the Canadian portion of the raising. FireFly finished our 10th September pricing cut-off at $1.76, leaving the new money with its nose just below water. For the biggest funding package of the fortnight, that’s not a bad opening act given the small discount. PC GOLD (ASX: PC2) Equity raised: $77 million

Advertisement

Price: $1.05 Discount: 7.9 per cent Current price: $1.06– up one per cent PC Gold didn’t need FireFly-sized pockets to make its point. The company secured $75 million from institutional investors. Its incoming directors also put their hands in their pockets for another $2 million, with both sources kicking in at $1.05 per share, a 7.9 per cent discount to the previous close and a 5.4 per cent discount to the five-day volume-weighted average price (VWAP). Wallabi Group acted as joint lead manager and sole bookrunner, with Hannam & Partners and Canaccord Genuity Australia (again) also joint lead managers.

Advertisement

The money gives PC Gold considerable firepower at its Spring Hill project in the Northern Territory’s Pine Creek gold province, where a July resource update delivered 1.51 million ounces at 1.1 grams per tonne (g/t), including one million ounces in the indicated category. Funds will support a major drilling campaign, feasibility work and underground infrastructure as PC Gold chases resource growth and a higher-grade underground opportunity. At $1.09 as at our 9th September cut-off date, punters were just one per cent in front, but hey, a win is a win. A big cheque, a single-digit discount and an aftermarket price above issue is the kind of raising that gets everyone leaving the room claiming a victory of sorts. EUREKA GROUP HOLDINGS (ASX: EGH)

Advertisement

Equity raised: $80.2 million Price: 61.5 cents Premium: 0.8 per cent Current price: 64 cents – up 4.1 per cent There is nothing quite like a capital raise done at a premium to market to get a stock moving north. Eureka Group nailed both a premium and a resultant market price lift after putting away $80m in our snapshot period.

Advertisement

The affordable rental accommodation operator launched a fully underwritten $80.2 million accelerated entitlement offer at 61.5 cents – slightly above its 61-cent pre-halt close and just 0.4 per cent below its five-day VWAP. The money is helping fund the company’s $123.8 million acquisition of the NSW Living Portfolio, delivering a refreshing industry change and some M&A rather than just another drill program. MA Moelis Australia Advisory, Morgans Corporate and Unified Capital Partners were bookrunners, underwriters and joint lead managers. And institutions didn’t blink. The institutional component raised $70.7 million, with eligible institutional shareholders taking up 95.1 per cent of their entitlements. The remaining retail component is expected to raise $9.5 million.

Advertisement

Eureka closed at 64 cents on 9th September – 4.1 per cent above the offer price. Paying above the last trade for new stock and still making money isn’t normally how the discount game works. Together, the headline trio accounted for $347.2 million, or just over half the money chased during the entire snapshot window. For the right stories, the equity window wasn’t merely open. Somebody had taken the hinges off. Not everyone received quite the same treatment though. Broken Hill Mines’ high-grade silver-lead-zinc Pinnacles mine located 15 kilometres southwest of Broken Hill,NSW.

Advertisement

Broken Hill Mines secured a fully underwritten $90 million package at 76 cents, a 10.1 per cent discount, to fund production growth, drilling and infrastructure at its 4.8Mt at 9.2 per cent zinc equivalent Centenary project in NSW and its 6Mt running 10.9 per cent zinc equivalent Pinnacles project just next door. Petra Capital was sole lead manager, bookrunner and underwriter, with Euroz Hartleys as co-lead manager, Blue Ocean Equities as co-manager and Peloton Capital acting as broker to the placement. At 68 cents by our cut-off date, however, investors were 10.5 per cent underwater - the same open equity window, but a slightly different view from the other side. Andean Silver raised $40 million at $2.45 to accelerate work towards a potential restart of its Cerro Bayo silver-gold asset in Chile. Canaccord and Euroz were joint lead managers and bookrunners, with Jett Capital Advisors as co-manager. The 13.7 per cent discount looked generous. The stock sat at $2.30 by our cut-off date, so everybody’s 6 per cent on the wrong side of the ledger. Falcon Metals raised $30 million at 60 cents for drilling at its Blue Moon and Errabiddy gold projects, with Canaccord, Jett and Bell Potter splitting the clip. The 11.8 per cent discount price didn’t quite hold, with the stock now at 54 cents and investors 10 per cent in the hole.

Advertisement

Then things got more interesting. Titomic raised $16.5 million at 13 cents for its US expansion and commercialisation push, with Canaccord and Peloton as joint lead managers and Bell Potter weighing in as co-manager. The brokers held Titomic’s feet to the flames and extracted a hefty 23.5 per cent discount but were rewarded when the shares reached 14.5 cents, up 11.5 per cent, but you had to be quick. It was chocolates to boiled lollies in the end, with the stock at 12.5 cents at Sept 10 cut-off date. Sierra Nevada Gold raised $12.85 million at 10 cents for drilling at its As Safra copper-gold project in Saudi Arabia, with Fosters Stockbroking and Argonaut pulling the punters together. At 14 cents, investors were already up a whopping 40 per cent. Nice work if you can get it! Black Bear Minerals secured $12.5 million at 55 cents, with Canaccord as sole lead manager and bookrunner, to advance its Shafter silver project in Texas. At 54 cents, the new money was just a touch underwater.

Advertisement

The small cap punters that regularly swing off the coat tails of CPS Capital overran the $3.5m West Coast Silver raise that quickly turned into a $6 million raise at 9.5 cents at a 13.8 per cent discount. Paul Cronin, who achieved superman status along with Eric DeMori when the pair listed and grew Adriatic Metals to about $1.8 billion, weighed in as a cornerstone on this one. CPS has been sweet on West Coast Silver ever since raising its initial bag of cash at close to 3 cents, and while 9.5 cents now looks like a big win, those that chose not to sell at the heady price of 29 cents in December last year probably don’t think so. The stock has come off a little post-raise but will accelerate work at the historic Elizabeth Hill silver project in WA that has some of the highest-grade silver occurrences on the planet. The discount rack got considerably busier further down the list. Core Energy Minerals raised $3.025 million at 0.6 cents – a 25 per cent discount to market – for exploration at its Nova uranium joint venture in Namibia.

Advertisement

Canaccord was lead manager, earning a six per cent cash fee and, subject to approvals, a lazy 25 million broker options. At 0.7 cents, the new money was sitting on a sweet 16.6 per cent gain. Castle Minerals went the other way, raising $4 million at 7.5 cents with Euroz as lead manager – only 2.6 per cent below its previous close and actually a 4.7 per cent premium to its 15-day VWAP – principally for its Nielle gold project in Côte d’Ivoire. The new money has its nose in front with the stock sitting at eight cents. Critical Resources raised $1.6 million at half a cent, including $475,000 from directors, to fund exploration across its NZ, Canadian and Aussie projects along with its battery tech. 62 Capital got the gig as lead manager for a six per cent fee and a sweet 24 million broker options. At 0.7 cents, placement investors were a whopping 40 per cent ahead. Mount Ridley Mines raised $2 million at 3.3 cents plus a $100,000 director commitment to advance its Grass Patch rare earths project and its Selectro processing technology. Alpine Capital led the raise at an eye-catching 17.5 per cent discount, with the new shares streaking as high as 5.4 cents and closing on our cut-off date at 4.2 cents, a satisfying 27 per cent hike.

Advertisement

Jameson Resources raised $5 million at 3.5 cents, with PAC Partners acting as lead manager and bookrunner. Its ticker is currently trading at 3.8 cents, so punters are generally happy. Alliance Aviation Services raised $40 million at 70 cents for working capital and debt reduction, with Barrenjoey Markets underwriting the raise. It is currently trading at 59.5 cents - ouch! - while 4DS Memory sought almost $5 million at one cent alongside its proposed Jenesys acquisition, an Australian software developer specialising in Edge-AI (artificial intelligence processed locally on a device rather than in the cloud, with Jason Skinner’s JP Equity Holdings as lead manager. Punters are on the fence with the company trading at the offer price. Not every company required a broker to go rattling the tin. Duxton Farms’ $9.74 million raising involved an entitlement offer of one convertible note for every 11 shares, paying 7.5 per cent a year. Prescient Therapeutics went directly to shareholders too through a $7 million SPP, while WIN Metals raised $860,000 through notes paying 10 per cent. The IPO market, with three new entrants, added another layer.

Advertisement

Almasar Minerals raised $12 million at 20 cents, with Oracle Capital Group and 708 Capital as joint lead managers. The newcomer traded as high as 28 cents before closing at 22.5 cents on September 10, leaving subscribers 12.5 per cent ahead. Axiant Resources raised $8 million in its IPO at 20 cents with Argonaut as lead manager and bookrunner. It traded as high as 23.5 cents before closing at 19 cents, putting subscribers close to break-even. Powerhaus Uranium floated at 20 cents, with Canaccord and Pamplona Capital as joint lead managers to put away $9.5m. Its September 10 close of 23 cents handed thrill-seekers a 15 per cent gain. Three new floats. Three pretty comfortable starts. While some established companies had to reach deep into the discount rack to fill their books, the new kids wasted little time showing some of the old hands how it was done.

Advertisement

And that brings us back to the brokers and, in summary: Canaccord emerged as the busiest house with nine mandates, ahead of Euroz on five and Argonaut on three in our snapshot. Those dollar figures overlap; FireFly alone appears in all three, so the mandate count remains the cleaner scoreboard. For the brokers, the old soft-shoe shuffle remained the same – find enough of a discount to make institutional clients reach for their cheque books while persuading company boards they haven’t just sold the family silver. But this last fortnight once again showed why the bookbuild isn’t the final scoreboard. Broken Hill and Alliance Aviation’s new investors were underwater. Sierra Nevada’s were up a third. Mount Ridley and Critical Resources were both up more than 30 per cent -nice. Eureka asked institutions to pay slightly more than the stock’s last trade, attracted a 95.1 per cent institutional take-up and then closed above the offer price.

Advertisement

And the new kids supplied their own lesson: Powerhaus was 15 per cent above issue, Almasar 12.5 per cent, with Axiant treading water as at the 10th of September. Thirty-five deals and $687.5 million later, there was little evidence the Australian equity market had lost its mojo. However, plenty of evidence proved appetite can come at wildly different prices. For companies, getting cash in the tin matters and for brokers, getting the book away matters. For investors, only one thing really counts – what happened after they wrote the cheque. NationalWAHomelessness ‘Where else are they supposed to go?’ Two-day deadline to clear Perth homeless camp sparks fierce backlash Carla Hildebrandt September 11, 2026 — 1:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Five people sleeping rough in Perth’s southern suburbs have been given two days to pack up their personal belongings and move on, sparking backlash on social media. The City of Rockingham notice, issued by the team leader of ranger services on Wednesday, gives the five people camping at Baldivis wetlands until midday on Friday to remove their belongings. The Baldvis wetlands is about 45 kilometres south of Perth. Trails WA/T Lindsey According to the notice, anything left behind would be “removed and impounded” and held for between three days to two months, before they would be “destroyed”. The notice does say why the people are being moved on, or offer any assistance, only that it is in accordance with the Local Government Act.

Advertisement

But Homeless in Perth WA’s Facebook page administrator, Vangy Baker, who is in touch with the people living at the wetlands, said the people who were issued the notice have no car to move their items. The notice issued to homeless people sleeping at the Baldivis wetlands. “Moving tents and belongings does not resolve homelessness. It simply moves people from one patch of land to another,” Baker said. “If smaller, isolated camps around Baldivis, Rockingham or anywhere else are cleared without appropriate alternative accommodation, there is a real risk that more people will gather at visible locations. “Where else are they supposed to go?” Vangy Baker

Advertisement

The small camp at Baldvis is separate to a larger well-known homeless camp in Safety Bay along Memorial Drive, where roughly 150 homeless people are living in tents and their cars. Baker said she was contacted several times daily by “desperate” people in Perth who have nowhere to stay. “They are exhausted and frightened. Many services don’t have beds available, and they are repeatedly calling services that are already full,” she said. “People are being punished for being visible, while the fundamental problem remains unchanged - they have nowhere lawful and safe to sleep. “At an absolute minimum, there should be lawful safe parking and temporary sleeping areas near tilers and showers and other safe facilities.”

Advertisement

Shelter WA chief executive Kath Snell. Shelter WA Kath Snell, the chief executive of Shelter WA, the peak body for ending homelessness, said this was another example of how the state needed “urgent housing solutions”. “Moving people on doesn’t end homelessness, it just relocates it, and that is why Rockingham desperately needs more safe, secure, affordable homes, as well as a dedicated respite service for people doing it tough,” Snell said. “This is sadly yet another example of how dire our housing crisis is and how urgent we need housing solutions, both respite and long-term.” The notice has drawn hundreds of reactions and emotional comments on social media.

“Not good enough. Where’s their compassion?” one person wrote. “This breaks my heart and makes me angry at the same time,” wrote another. One person said it was the most “bloody appalling thing I’ve seen all year”. Others wanted to know why the notice had been issued in the first place. title: Superannuation is too important for populism
text:
Advertisement
